Building the AAA Lighting Pipeline in Three.js
From the G-buffer to temporal upscaling, here is each stage of the lightmap, probe and screen-space reflection pipeline measured against Three.js: what games require of it, what Three.js has today, and the pull requests in review or still to write.
Ben Houston • • 21 min read
Part 2 picked a pipeline for indoor scenes: lightmaps, light probes and reflection probes, with SSR, SSGI and ambient occlusion on top. Here I measure Three.js against it one stage at a time: what the games require, what Three.js has, and what is missing.
The pipeline#
The pipeline has two parts. The setup fills three caches: lightmaps for static meshes, a light probe grid for moving objects, and reflection probes for each room.
Each frame then reads those caches and adds the screen-space work on top:
Where things stand#
The biggest remaining gaps are in the SSR, SSGI and BRDF rows: Hi-Z tracing and coverage for SSR, the same coverage for SSGI, and above all the pluggable indirect lighting that ties both cascades into the BRDF.
It has moved this fast because of the Three.js maintainers. Michael Herzog (@Mugen87) has reviewed most of these PRs, and more than once has reworked one into a better design that fits how Three.js as a whole is built, adjusting the renderer's internals to make room for it. mrdoob has expressed strong support for many of them. I am very lucky to have both.
So far, though, these pieces have been proposed and reviewed one at a time. Nobody has been asked to sign up to the whole. This series is my attempt to put them together into one picture, so that each PR can be judged for where it fits as well as for what it does.
The pipeline, stage by stage#
The G-buffer#
What the games require. SSR, GTAO and the denoisers run in screen space before lighting, so they need per-pixel depth, normals, roughness, metalness and motion vectors. A deferred engine also stores base color and emissive, because its lighting pass reads only the G-buffer. Three.js renders forward and its beauty pass reads those from the material, so the G-buffer fits in 16 bytes per pixel. Part 2 has the layout and the memory budget for the whole frame.
What Three.js has. WebGPURenderer already renders a G-buffer prepass with multiple render targets, and the SSR examples use it today:
const scenePass = pass( scene, camera );
scenePass.setMRT( mrt( {
	output: output,
	diffuseColor: vec4( diffuseColor.rgb, materialMetalness ),
	normal: vec4( packNormalToRGB( normalView ).rgb, materialRoughness ),
	velocity: velocity
} ) );
What is missing. Normal precision. SSR is unforgiving of normal error: a ray reflected off a slightly wrong normal lands somewhere visibly wrong at the end of a long trace. With RGB8 normals, smooth curved surfaces snap to a limited set of directions, and their reflections show banding and clumping.
AAA G-buffers use octahedral encoding: fold the sphere of directions onto an octahedron, unfold it into a square, and store two coordinates. It is the most accurate of the encodings surveyed by Cigolle et al. for its size. PR #35480 adds packNormalToOctahedral() and unpackOctahedralToNormal():
RG16 snorm is the target, with RG16F as the fallback.
Global illumination#
What the games require. Bounce light baked into lightmaps for everything that does not move, and a probe volume to light dynamic objects, ideally one that does not leak light through walls.
What Three.js has. Every standard material takes a lightMap, and there is now a complete baking pipeline in the browser to make one; that is Part 4. For dynamic objects, LightProbeGrid places a grid of probes through a scene, each storing incoming light as L2 spherical harmonics, and lights each object from the probes around it (example).
The grid's limit was how long a capture took. Profiling showed the bake was CPU-bound on submitting render passes, so the batched capture renders eight probes per pass with one array camera, and a resolution-12 grid dropped from 5.6 s to 1.2 s. Culling each draw against its own sub-camera doubled that again. The grid now bakes about eight times faster than it did at the start of September, fast enough to re-capture a few probes per frame, and supports multi-bounce light. Integrating the spherical harmonics exactly also cut their error from 2.4% to 0.08%.
What is missing. Probes leak. A probe on one side of a wall can light an object on the other, so a dark room glows with the light of the bright room next door. DDGI solves this by storing, with each probe, the distance to the nearest surface in every direction, and ignoring probes that cannot see the point being lit. I have DDGI-style visibility weighting working as a draft PR. Testing visibility against all eight surrounding probes was costly, so the draft can use tetrahedral interpolation, which blends four:
Ambient and specular occlusion#
What the games require. Lightmaps are too coarse for contact shadows, and they know nothing about dynamic objects. Games add screen-space occlusion on top, and Activision's GTAO is the standard. It also produces a bent normal, the average open direction, which gives specular occlusion (GTSO): a reflection pointing into a fold of the surface is occluded, one pointing out of the opening is not.
Horizon-based SSGI, which is what Three.js has, runs the same depth-buffer search as GTAO and gathers light along the way. With SSGI on, its pass supplies the occlusion and the bent normal, and GTAO runs only when SSGI is off.
Which light the occlusion applies to matters as much as how it is computed. Occlusion is a shared buffer, set with builtinAOContext, and each source decides whether to read it:
- The lightmap, probe grid and environment apply AO to their indirect diffuse, combined with the material's AO map as min( materialAO, gtao ).
- The reflection probes and environment apply GTSO to their indirect specular.
- SSR and SSGI apply neither. A screen-space hit is something the ray found, so it is already correctly occluded.
- Behind SSGI, the diffuse sources skip AO. SSGI's coverage is the share of the hemisphere that something on screen blocks, which is the occlusion itself. The cascade already scales the lightmap or probe grid by 1 − coverage.
- Occlusion darkens a source's color and leaves its coverage alone. Lowering an occluded probe's coverage would let the next source's unoccluded light leak into the corner.
What Three.js has. GTAO already feeds the lighting through a context, which is the pattern the indirect lighting design in Part 5 extends:
const aoPass = ao( prePassDepth, prePassNormal, camera );
scenePass.contextNode = builtinAOContext( aoPass.getTextureNode().sample( screenUV ).r );
What is missing.
- Specular occlusion. GTAO outputs a single visibility value, and the lighting model turns it into specular occlusion with a heuristic. It does not know which directions are blocked, so metal keeps reflecting the sky inside folds. Bent normals and GTSO are up as a draft PR. The bent normal comes out of the same horizon search; the cost is an AO target that grows from one byte per pixel to four.
- Edge-aware upsampling. Half-resolution GTAO upsampled bilinearly leaves dark outlines around objects. jointBilateralUpsample() uses the full-resolution depth and normals as guides (Kopf et al. 2007), so the result stops at the edges. It is drafted and not yet submitted; half-resolution SSR and SSGI need the same filter.
- Bent normals from SSGINode, so that specular occlusion does not need a second pass when SSGI is on.
Screen-space reflections#
SSR has its own series, Fixing Three.js's Screen Space Reflections. This section is the summary.
What the games require. Shipped engines agree on a recipe, set out with its sources in How Games Do Screen-Space Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead. In a cascade, SSR has to:
- Trace the previous frame's lit image, so the reflection exists before the frame is shaded.
- Trace exactly over any distance, using a Hi-Z depth pyramid.
- Trace at half resolution and reuse rays between pixels, which is what brings the trace under a millisecond.
- Output radiance and coverage, so the probes can fill what it misses.
- Denoise that radiance and coverage, and leave the BRDF to the material.
What Three.js has. SSRNode importance-samples the full GGX lobe with correct Fresnel, can validate and refine its hits, and its result is reprojected and accumulated over time. The trace is a fixed-step march with short rays. The three SSR examples find 98%, 82% and 46% of the hits within their own ray length, in 2 to 3 ms, and the denoiser fills the gaps from neighbouring pixels. The result is composited over the image, as in the SSR example:
const litColor = scenePassColor.rgb.add( denoisedReflections.rgb );
What is missing. All five requirements, each prototyped or in review except ray reuse.
Exact tracing. A Hi-Z pyramid is a mip chain where each texel stores the nearest depth of the four below it. The ray takes large steps through empty space at coarse levels and single-pixel steps near surfaces, so it finds every hit the depth buffer contains and has no maximum distance to tune. My implementation adds a HiZNode that builds the pyramid in a compute pass. Trace time at 1920×1080, against the fixed-step march raised to the same hit rate:
That is still a ray for every pixel. Tracing at half resolution with a joint bilateral upsample is written, and ray reuse between pixels, as Frostbite does it, is still to build. Exact Screen-Space Reflections on a Budget has the full plan.
Coverage. Today a ray that misses samples an environment map inside SSR: an equirectangular texture passed in as environmentNode, which cannot be the PMREM-filtered scene.environment, let alone a local probe. Adding SSR over the image also counts the environment reflection twice. In a cascade, SSR outputs one thing: radiance premultiplied by coverage, with coverage 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss, and fading toward the screen border. The environment input and the BRDF estimate leave the node. This is prototyped as part of Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
Tracing the previous frame. SSR cannot be part of the lighting while it reads the lighting's output. DOOM's answer is to trace the current depth buffer but read colors from the previous frame: reproject each hit point into last frame's TRAA output and sample it there. A hit that fails the check against last frame's depth gets zero coverage. Last frame's image already contained last frame's reflections, so a mirror facing a mirror gains a bounce each frame. Previous-frame tracing is in review.
The loop needs two rules. The image SSR reads must be linear HDR radiance, taken after TRAA but before tone mapping and bloom, or reflections pick up tone-mapped colors and bloom halos. And the fed-back radiance must be clamped, because each frame's reflections become the next frame's input and a single firefly compounds frame after frame.
Denoising. Three.js has two reflection denoisers. The pair the SSR example runs, TemporalReprojectNode and RecurrentDenoiseNode, reads every black pixel as missing data and fills it from its neighbours. That hides the tracer's misses and leaves nothing for the probes to answer. zalo's SVGF-based DenoiseNode replaced the pair in the SSR example and was taken back out five days later. I traced the flicker that caused it to the missing coverage: at the edge of a reflection a hit and a miss were averaged as two samples of one signal, and the history kept resetting.
My ssr-coverage branch carries coverage through every stage of DenoiseNode and takes its statistics from covered samples only. Still to do are a two-lookup history, a history cap that follows roughness, and skipping mirrors and matte pixels. The denoiser filters incoming light and the material applies its BRDF afterwards, so it needs no albedo in the G-buffer and no demodulation step. How Games Denoise Reflections, and What Three.js Does Instead has the comparison and the plan.
Screen-space global illumination#
What the games require. Engines that use SSGI as part of their lighting put it in front of their baked light as the first stage of the diffuse cascade. That means SSGI has to output coverage, trace the previous frame's lit image, and accumulate over time at half resolution.
What Three.js has. SSGINode is built on the visibility-bitmask approach of SSRT3, which extends GTAO's horizon search to gather light as well as occlusion. One search of 24 depth samples yields a GI texture and an AO texture, and it is much less noisy than a single random ray, because each sample accounts for a whole arc of directions. The SSGI example traces the current frame's beauty pass and composites over it.
What is missing.
- Coverage output. The sectors the search marks as blocked are the directions in which it found a surface, so coverage is 1 − ao, and the node already computes it. What is missing is handing the GI and that coverage to the cascade as a pair, so SSGI can replace the baked bounce where it has an answer.
- Previous-frame tracing. SSR reads the previous frame once per pixel, where its ray lands. SSGI reads it at every sample that finds a surface, so reprojecting at each read is paid many times per pixel. A draft measures the options on an Apple M3:
The third option also follows moving objects, and shows no visible artifacts in the test scenes.
Reflection probes#
What the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.
What Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.
What is missing.
- A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
- Fast access to many probes. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, and the texture class is in review.
- Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so a dark corner or the inside of a cupboard reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both. Still to do.
- Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is enough for blurry room reflections, since SSR handles the sharp ones, and takes a quarter of the memory. Still to do.
Indirect lighting in the BRDF#
What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:
- Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage, then the lightmap on static meshes or the probe grid on everything else, then the environment map.
- Indirect specular: SSR, then the box-projected probes, then the environment map.
Three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.
What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.
What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
TRAA and TAAU#
What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.
What Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:
scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );
const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );
TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.
What is missing.
- Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:
- Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.
- TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.
- Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.
Future work#
- Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise costs about 400 operations per sample, on every pixel, every frame. I want to move some of that into a small map generated at startup, so each sample is a lookup and a few adds.
- Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, and Three.js does not have it yet.
- A physically based sun and sky. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky in real units that agree with each other and with the exposure. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
- Reflection probes in glTF. There is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load.
- Directional lightmaps. The lightmaps here store one irradiance value per texel, so normal maps cannot respond to baked light. The options are an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.

The third option also follows moving objects, and shows no visible artifacts in the test scenes.
Reflection probes#
What the games require. Indoors, one environment map is wrong: walk from a red room into a blue corridor and the floor should reflect red, then blue. Every game in the survey, and Unreal's reflection captures, use local reflection probes: cubemaps captured inside each room, each with a box describing the volume it influences. Inside its box a probe is box-projected, which removes most of a cubemap's parallax error (Lagarde's write-up is the classic explanation). Where boxes overlap, probes blend.
What Three.js has. CubeCamera captures a cubemap, PMREMGenerator prefilters it, and getParallaxCorrectNormal() box-projects it, as the box-projected environment map example shows. That is one probe per material, set by hand.
What is missing.
- A probe system. Box-projected reflection probes for WebGPURenderer adds scene-level probes with influence boxes and blending, and is up as a draft PR.
- Fast access to many probes. Cube array textures put every probe in one texture; sampling them is merged, and the texture class is in review.
- Probe normalization. A probe is captured at one point in a room, so a dark corner or the inside of a cupboard reflects a brightly lit room. Call of Duty's fix, introduced in Black Ops II and carried into Infinite Warfare, is to scale the probe's reflection by the ratio of the diffuse light at the pixel to the diffuse light at the probe. The lightmaps and probe grid already provide both. Still to do.
- Small probes. PMREMGenerator has a minimum size of 256². A 128² probe is enough for blurry room reflections, since SSR handles the sharp ones, and takes a quarter of the memory. Still to do.
Indirect lighting in the BRDF#
What the games require. The bounced light has to go through the material's BRDF, so Fresnel, roughness and metalness apply to it as they do to direct light. In a forward renderer the beauty pass needs two inputs:
- Indirect diffuse: SSGI where it has coverage, then the lightmap on static meshes or the probe grid on everything else, then the environment map.
- Indirect specular: SSR, then the box-projected probes, then the environment map.
Three.js renders forward, so SSR, SSGI and AO are computed before the beauty pass and each material reads them while it shades. Tracing the previous frame is what makes that order possible.
What Three.js has. Indirect diffuse is mostly in place: lightMap, LightProbeGrid and scene.environment all feed it, and AO reaches it through builtinAOContext. Indirect specular comes only from scene.environment, or a material's own envMap.
What is missing. A way to plug a screen-space result, or a cascade of sources, into a material's indirect specular, the way AO is plugged into its diffuse. This is the biggest gap in the pipeline, and my proposed design is in Pluggable Indirect Lighting for Three.js.
TRAA and TAAU#
What the games require. Temporal anti-aliasing whose output can also be next frame's input to SSR and SSGI, so it has to stay sharp under motion and must not feed ghosts or fireflies back into the reflections. Every engine this series measures itself against also renders below the output resolution and reconstructs the difference over time: TSR in Unreal, FSR 2 in Godot, DLSS and FSR in Cyberpunk 2077.
What Three.js has. A TRAA node with Halton jitter, motion-vector reprojection and variance clipping of the history, and TAAUNode, which follows Karis's temporal supersampling and FSR 2. The TAAU example shows it at a quarter of the pixels:
scenePass.setResolutionScale( 0.5 );
const taauNode = taau( scenePassColor, scenePassDepth, scenePassVelocity, camera );
TAAU takes TRAA's place as the last stage of the frame. Everything before it runs at the render resolution, its linear HDR output is what the next frame's SSR and SSGI read, and bloom and tone mapping run after it. At a scale of 0.5, the screen buffers at 1080p drop from about 157 MB to 81 MB.
What is missing.
- Wider clipping at rest. Variance clipping stops ghosting by rejecting history that no longer matches the current frame, and it also rejects good history. TRAA tightens its clip box to 0.5σ under fast motion, but at rest the box was 1σ, tight enough to clip converged sub-pixel detail, so a still image never fully resolved and longer histories scored worse. A drafted change widens the box to 2σ at rest and adds a historyLength control. Against a supersampled reference:
- Sharper history. History sampled bilinearly blurs a little more every frame the camera moves. Catmull-Rom history sampling, a draft PR, keeps it sharp. Both refinements apply to TAAU as well.
- TAAU in the full pipeline. The example upscales a single scene pass. The pipeline has a prepass, half-resolution effects and a beauty pass that all have to agree on resolution and jitter, and none of that has been tried together yet. With TAAU at 0.5, half-resolution SSR and SSGI would run at a quarter of the output resolution on each axis, so it may be better to run them at the full render resolution and skip the bilateral upsample.
- Texture mip bias. Rendering at half resolution makes the GPU pick blurrier texture mips than the output deserves. Temporal upscalers pair with a negative mip bias of about log2 of the resolution scale, and Three.js does not apply one yet.
Future work#
- Cheaper noise. Houston Stratified Noise costs about 400 operations per sample, on every pixel, every frame. I want to move some of that into a small map generated at startup, so each sample is a lookup and a few adds.
- Auto-exposure. Walking from a dark room into a bright courtyard needs eye adaptation, and Three.js does not have it yet.
- A physically based sun and sky. A room lit through its windows needs a sun and sky in real units that agree with each other and with the exposure. A prototype does single scattering; multiple scattering and clouds are still to do.
- Reflection probes in glTF. There is no standard way to ship reflection probes. The minimum is each probe's position and influence box, so a loader can capture the probes on load.
- Directional lightmaps. The lightmaps here store one irradiance value per texel, so normal maps cannot respond to baked light. The options are an ambient term plus one dominant direction as in The Last of Us and Call of Duty, L1 spherical harmonics as in Frostbite, or spherical Gaussians as in The Order: 1886.

This shredded Brussels sprout and arugula salad is crisp, refreshing and filling. Enjoy this simple recipe for dinner, pack it for lunch tomorrow, make it for the holidays! Recipe yields 4 large portions or 6 to 8 side salads.
Pear Salad with Walnuts
This fresh green salad with pears, walnuts, dates and blue cheese is a fresh option for your holiday table! It’s a great side salad for fall dinners, too. Recipe yields 4 side salads.
Butternut Tabbouleh
This fresh winter tabbouleh salad recipe features butternut squash instead of tomatoes, along with some dried cranberries for complementary flavor. This recipe yields 4 side salads. Feel free to double the recipe; if you do, you’ll likely need to cook the butternut squash longer than indicated below.
Autumn Kale Salad with Fennel, Honeycrisp and Goat Cheese
Healthy kale salad featuring shaved fennel, chopped honeycrisp apple, toasted pepitas, dried cranberries and goat cheese, tossed in a lemony dressing. This recipe yields 2 large, full-meal salads or 4 side salads.
The Little Green Salad
This simple green side salad is made with Parmesan and toasted nuts, tossed in lemon dressing. It’s wonderful in its simplest form, but you can add my suggested seasonal variations or put your own spin on it. Recipe yields 6 to 8 side salads.
Balsamic Butternut, Kale and Cranberry Panzanella
This winter panzanella salad features roasted butternut squash, kale, toasted croutons, cranberries and shallots tossed in homemade balsamic vinaigrette. Recipe yields 3 to 4 meal-sized salads.

Apple reveals new Mac security controls as AI agents raise privacy risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:01:02 UTC
06:01:02 KST

As promised last month, Apple on Monday announced changes to Mac security controls designed to protect users’ data from the growing popularity of AI agents and their apps’ demand for “full disk access.”
“Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk,” Apple warned in its blog post aimed at app developers.
Unlike AI chatbots that simply answer questions, agents run on a user’s device where they can take actions across the operating system, files, and apps on the user’s behalf.
While the tools can be useful, Apple has grown concerned about the increased risks to users’ data and privacy that these AI agents introduce. At the same time, the company has been benefiting from sales of Mac minis and Mac Studio computers that AI early adopters have been purchasing specifically to run their local AI models.
To balance these competing interests, Apple said in October that it would revise some of its security settings around Mac apps. The announcement followed two notable incidents involving AI agents. In one, a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app read their private messages without consent; a separate report from Wired cited a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app that could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.
Now, Apple is sharing the changes it’s making.
For starters, it’s splitting up Device Control and Data Access into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The changes are designed to help users better understand that selecting the first option means overriding built-in security protections.
To streamline configurations, Apple says there will now also be a single method for granting permissions that involves selecting the requested app from a list. The company will also introduce new guidance encouraging users to grant access only to the specific apps that need it when they enable the System & App Protection Override setting. Similar guidance will appear when users enable Full Disk Access to allow an app to access their folders.
The company will also provide users with “increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted,” the blog post notes.
Another change will give users more granular control over when an AI agent or app can gain access by allowing users to configure their apps to ask for permission every time access is needed. While arguably tedious and a potential obstacle to true automation, the feature could allow users to experiment with local AI without giving the agent carte blanche.
There will also be a new transparency indicator that appears when an app is controlling another app through the System & App Protection Override option.
The changes, which are arriving with macOS 27.3, don’t appear to prevent Mac users from installing and running AI agents or other apps that ask for higher levels of access. Instead, they give users more nuanced options, control, and information about the choices they’re making.
Apple advises app developers to adjust their onboarding processes to account for the new changes and suggests that their apps learn to “gracefully handle having access to only a limited set of folders or apps.”
Developers of apps that request Full Disk Access for disk backup or to provide assistive technologies can request exceptions to the new rules (which Apple calls “entitlements”) to preserve the same functionality they offered before the macOS 27.3 update.

Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park (www1.wdr.de) 62
			
		 	
				Slashdot readers djgl and Mirnotoriety shared a story about how a Microsoft Outlook outage contributed to a chlorine leak at Germany's Phantasialand theme park, injuring 15 guests, four of whom were hospitalized. German broadcasting institution WDR reports (translated to English):  We were all affected by this problem: On Friday, there was a disruption that crippled the US software company Microsoft, including its email program Outlook. Phantasialand was also affected. Due to the disruption, no emails were received, as the company informed WDR on Saturday. As a result, no one was aware that the sauna area's maintenance safety system had already issued an email alert. This was because the automatic dosing system had pumped too much chlorine into the pool.
Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Bruhl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday. Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15.  Cybersecurity architect and computer scientist Stephan Skrobisch said Microsoft is not responsible for the incident. "It's clearly the system's design that's the problem. They failed to implement an additional notification mechanism."
Slashdot reader davidwr agrees, writing in a comment: "Proper alarms would be a hardwired alarm that would be visible or audiable to someone who was on-site who could've gotten everyone out of the water. The blame for the injuries goes to the water park and/or whatever consultant told them it was okay not to have an on-site, hardwired alarm."

Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:48:08 UTC
05:48:08 KST

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi is “fiber-powered.”
“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”
While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.
In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.
AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”
AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.
AT&T: Fiber-powered is “literally false”
AT&T’s lawsuit said that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”

Caltech professor no longer grades homework's because everyone uses AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:47:53 UTC
05:47:53 KST

Professor Yi Ni had no laptop or projector. He instead rapidly filled eight blackboards with chalk scrawl during an introductory math class at Caltech on Friday.
Though the instruction was entirely analog, the specter of AI loomed large.
Ni, a professor at Caltech for 17 years, told me that he no longer grades homework on accuracy because students are using AI to complete it. Now, he grades it only on completion.
"There is a problem in the education process," Ni said. "Virtually all the homework in college math, you can use AI."
Chatbots, once derided for their inability to perform such basic tasks as counting the r's in "strawberry," can now do math as well as a graduate student.
And if you're an undergraduate student, that's kind of a big deal. Some, Business Insider has reported, are reconsidering whether to study math at all.
From my perch near the back of the lecture hall on Friday, however, I didn't see any students prompting ChatGPT.
In many ways, the class resembled a typical early morning university lecture (for undergrads, 10 a.m. is basically the crack of dawn). Sweatshirted students arrived late and filtered in the upper rows, while the overachievers sat in the front and asked questions.
Many bent their heads over large iPads and took furious notes while Yi filled up blackboard after blackboard with formulas and practice problems. Some had no note-taking materials to speak of. A couple closed their eyes for extended periods.
The class is a "core requirement" in Caltech's curriculum, meaning everyone at the school has to take it. Students I spoke to afterward gave a variety of majors, but none said they were comfortable speaking on the record.
So later on I spoke with Sathvik Redrouthu, a sophomore who'd taken the class last year. Redrouthu, a math major, said he didn't use AI because he wanted to understand the concepts.
"I was interested in the class," he said, adding that mainlining the homework with AI is like "shooting yourself in the foot" for when an in-person exam comes around.
"I personally think that if you leave AI out, then it pushes the average student to learn properly," he said.
If you're not interested in math, though, Redrouthu said you'd probably turn to AI — and you'd get away with it, until the exam at least.
Ni told me that, as a professor, he can't tell whether a problem set he assigns is completed using AI. It's unlike AI-generated writing, which is usually a pretty obvious amalgamation of short sentences, em dashes, and hypophora.
But math is all numbers: the specialty of AI programs.
Caltech has no unified guidance for how math professors should plan around AI now. Redrouthu said that this year, some of his classes come with an auspicious caveat: "AI allowed."
"Syllabuses are changing," he said.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:46:01 UTC
05:46:01 KST

California is suing OpenAI after its AI agents broke out of their testing environment and hacked other companies, including Hugging Face. In a lawsuit filed Monday, Attorney General Rob Bonta accuses OpenAI of violating consumer safety law by knowingly developing a “dangerous product without proper oversight,” as reported earlier by Reuters.
California sues OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
OpenAI lost control of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing, California’s AG claims.
The lawsuit claims the cyberattack on Hugging Face “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.” It alleges that OpenAI recently told the attorney general’s office that it “lost control” of its AI agents more than 80 times during testing.
After revealing the rogue AI attack on Hugging Face in July, news of several other similar incidents emerged, including attacks on an Australian government website, a German wiki site, and the software package manager RubyGems. OpenAI’s agents also tried to “bruteforce” a United Nations website.
“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-world cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta says in the press release. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”
OpenAI released its new cybersecurity AI model earlier this month, saying that it’s less likely to go rogue and attack other platforms. It’s also giving safety evaluators at Apollo Research access to its AI systems as part of a pilot program that monitors models for misalignment.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in an emailed statement to The Verge. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:42:51 UTC
05:42:51 KST

Uber Eats is officially launching drone delivery in partnership with Zipline starting Tuesday. The initial rollout begins in the Houston suburb of Spring, Texas, with Dallas next in line and dozens of additional US cities planned.
Uber and Zipline’s drone delivery service takes flight in Houston
Customers in Spring, Texas can now have orders from Jersey Mike’s, Zaxby’s, and local restaurants lowered into their yards via tethered pods—no tipping required.
The rollout comes after Uber and Zipline first announced their tie-up, including an investment in Zipline by Uber, back in August 2026. The companies have set the ambitious goal to hit 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029.
Spring residents in the coverage area will see a new “Drone” icon in the Uber app’s home screen to browse participating restaurants. At checkout, customers will need to confirm a clear drop-off zone in the yard, and can track the drone in real-time via the app. Because the system is fully autonomous, tipping is disabled — though customers can still rate the experience in the app.
Unlike other low-hovering delivery drones, Zipline’s aircraft cruise at over 300 feet at speeds up to 70 mph. The drone hovers high overhead and lowers a tethered delivery pod onto the customer’s doorstep or yard. The drones dynamically calculate flight paths based on wind, altitude, and speed — dipping their noses to accelerate or pitching upward to brake as quietly as possible. The drones are built to fly in rain and poor weather, carrying up to 8 pounds of cargo within a 10-mile radius of the restaurant.
The initial plan is to operate daily from 8AM to 10PM, Uber says. Customers can order from national chains like Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, alongside dozens of Houston-area staples such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal.
To be sure, the “1 million deliveries a day by 2029” target is very aggressive, especially considering that Zipline currently averages roughly one delivery every 20 seconds globally, or around 4,300 a day. Still, delivery drones are becoming a more widely adopted technology in many communities across the US, with Uber competing alongside other players like Amazon Prime Air and Google-backed Wing.

Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:29:48 UTC
05:29:48 KST

Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic (
https://axonnic.com
). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots.
Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA
We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly.
The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors.
When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks.
We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies.
Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension.
Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings.
So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG.
If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks!

Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers

Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave.
Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
They may have a point.
They may have a point.
“I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said.
Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors.
Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate.
Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”)
Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said.
Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale.
Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation.
“The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.”
Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about.
In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle.
In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth.
For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life.
Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills.
Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for.
On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.”
“The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.”
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns.
Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity.
That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat.
Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.)
Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses.
And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan.
It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US.
That’s not lost on Dominguez.
“Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
20:27:58 UTC
05:27:58 KST

Fossil fuels are still the biggest source of electricity for hyperscale data centers in the US, a new paper published in the journal Nature Sustainability shows. They likely burn through more electricity collectively than many countries do, resulting in a serious amount of greenhouse gas emissions.
US data centers now burn more electricity than a midsized country
The latest numbers are in on how much energy hyperscale data centers use and the carbon pollution they create.
The study homes in on hyperscale facilities — the massive structures spanning millions of square feet that developers are racing to build in large part to support generative AI. Researchers say the findings show that there’s a lot of work left to do to cut down pollution stemming from AI’s reliance on fossil fuels.
“We tend to discuss AI’s environmental footprint as though it were some fixed property of the technology, when in reality the same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it,” Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the new study and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, says in an email to The Verge. “I actually find that encouraging, because it means these impacts aren’t inevitable. We have choices about where we build and how we power this infrastructure.”
“The same computing infrastructure can have dramatically different consequences depending on the electricity system supporting it.”
Guidi and his team used satellite imagery to identify 403 hyperscale data centers in the US, estimating each facility’s power consumption based on its electrical capacity. Using data from the Environmental Protection Agency, they approximated how much carbon pollution each data center would have produced if connected to the local power grid between May 2024 and April 2025.
Altogether, the 403 hyperscale facilities likely consumed around 82 terawatt-hours of electricity that year, about 1.8 percent of all US electricity consumption. That’s even more than the amount of electricity that about 148 nations — a majority of the countries in the world including Austria, Israel, and Venezuela but excluding the largest economies including the US and China — individually burn through each year, according to John Sterman, director of the MIT System Dynamics group and MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative.
Electricity demand from these data centers produced 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 emissions, comparable to the annual carbon footprint of Denmark, according to the research paper. Sterman says that exceeds the total carbon emissions of about 113 nations. That’s because about 54 percent of the electricity the hyperscale facilities consumed likely came from gas and coal.
Sterman, who was not involved in the research with Guidi, disclosed that he used the help of Claude to compare the paper’s findings to electricity use and emissions of countries. “I think AI can be extraordinarily helpful,” Sterman says. “But we’ve got to figure out a way to limit the harms … Especially because those impacts are irreversible. Once you allow these data centers to emit the CO2, you can never undo that.”
Sterman says policymakers should require data center operators to bring new clean energy online. The study doesn’t account for local air pollution that can result from new gas infrastructure that’s being built to meet data center demand, or gas turbines that some AI companies have installed at their facilities to power themselves without connecting to the grid. And while hyperscale data centers encompass more than just AI-related computing, they also make up just a fraction of the thousands of data centers in the US — with more cropping up each year.
The study showed how big a difference the local electricity mix makes when it comes to the environmental impact of AI and data centers. Generating electricity in heavily coal-reliant Wyoming led to roughly seven times more carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour than in hydropower-rich Oregon. “Two data centers consuming exactly the same amount of electricity can have dramatically different carbon footprints simply because of where they’re located,” Guidi writes.
Fengqi You, a professor in energy systems engineering at Cornell University who was also not involved in the study, says the results highlight the problem of “long-term carbon lock-in.” “Power plants and supporting infrastructure built to meet rapidly growing data center demand may operate for decades. Decisions made today could therefore shape emissions well into the future,” You says in an email to The Verge.
Both You and Guidi also pointed out how problematic it is that researchers have to go through such great lengths to estimate energy consumption because data center operators won’t disclose that information. To that end, Guidi and his colleagues are using their research to build a website to track the environmental impact of individual data centers. A bipartisan bill making its way through Congress could also mandate greater disclosures nationally on data centers’ electricity use.
“Communities and policymakers need reliable, independent data on what these facilities mean for our air, health, and the climate. This study is an important step.” Gina McCarthy, former White House national climate advisor and EPA administrator, said in a statement shared by the research authors.
