How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
19:29:17 UTC
04:29:17 KST

How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and QPACK
A hands-on look at intercepting HTTP/3. How QUIC streams and QPACK work, what a proxy really sees, how to read and edit a request, and why the QPACK dynamic table makes some requests hard to read.
InterceptSuite Team
Short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.
In this post: curl is easy to edit because it does not use QPACK's dynamic table. Browsers do, so later requests arrive as table references you cannot read one row at a time. You can still forward, drop and replay them, and an edited request works on a fresh connection.
In this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.
Table of contents
A note on the tool: it shows raw bytes, and an extension decodes HTTP/3
This post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core shows raw bytes.
To read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.
What changes with HTTP/3
If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.
1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.
2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.
3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):
In HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).
One more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.
Why your usual proxy setup does not work
HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.
SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.
That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:
- The app (or a library) speaks SOCKS5 UDP itself. The lab client later in this post does this, so you can see exactly what the proxy receives.
- You redirect the app's traffic from outside the app, so it does not need to know about the proxy. This is what we use for curl and Edge. ProxyBridge does this on its own. InterceptSuite also has a Redirect tab, which is built on ProxyBridge and works inside the app.
For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.
Setup: the Redirect tab
Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line says Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.
A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.
These two demos show the Redirect tab and the CA install on each system:
Want to follow along? There is a 7-day trial for Windows, macOS and Linux.
Real traffic 1: curl
curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:
winget install cURL.cURL
The new build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).
curl --http3-only -sS -D - https://cloudflare-quic.com/cdn-cgi/trace
--http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output showed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.
In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:
The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:
Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:
The test site prints back what it saw. The first run says uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:
uag=edited-by-proxy
So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:
Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:
QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.
Real traffic 2: Browser traffic
Browsers are harder, for two reasons.
- ECH (Encrypted Client Hello). The real site name is hidden inside the handshake. The proxy only sees the CDN's public name, so it makes a certificate for the wrong name and the browser rejects it.
- Chromium does not run QUIC with a locally added CA. Even when Windows trusts the CA, Chromium refuses QUIC on a certificate that chains to a user-installed CA.
The fix is to start the browser with three flags:
msedge.exe --disable-features=EncryptedClientHello,UseDnsHttpsSvcb
           --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash>
           --origin-to-force-quic-on=*
- --disable-features=... turns off ECH and stops the browser from reading HTTPS DNS records, where the ECH keys come from.
- --origin-to-force-quic-on=* makes Edge try QUIC straight away, instead of waiting for an Alt-Svc header. * means every host. Use host:443 for one site.
- --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<hash> trusts QUIC connections signed by the InterceptSuite CA. Use this flag and not --ignore-certificate-errors.
<hash> is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:
openssl x509 -in intercept-ca.pem -pubkey -noout | openssl pkey -pubin -outform der | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64
Edge shows a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.
With the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page says "your browser used HTTP/3":
In InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:
And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:
The response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body shows as HTML.
Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:
Edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.
How SOCKS5 carries UDP
UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.
- The client opens a normal TCP connection to the proxy, does the SOCKS5 greeting, and sends the command 03 (UDP ASSOCIATE). The proxy answers with an address and a port. This is the UDP relay.
- The client sends UDP datagrams to that relay address. Each datagram starts with a small header, then the real payload.
The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:
RSV (2 bytes) | FRAG (1) | ATYP (1) | DST.ADDR (variable) | DST.PORT (2) | DATA
The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.
InterceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.
The lab: seeing every byte
Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.
- Server: a small HTTP/3 server on 127.0.0.1:4433 with a self-signed certificate. It answers with JSON that repeats what it received (method, path, one custom header, and the body). It also prints what it got, so you can see what actually arrived.
- Client: an HTTP/3 client that sends its datagrams through the SOCKS5 UDP relay. aioquic does not know about SOCKS5, so the client wraps its datagrams itself. This is the whole trick:
class Shim(asyncio.DatagramProtocol):
    """Wraps each QUIC datagram in the SOCKS5 UDP header."""
    def sendto(self, data, addr=None):
        hdr = b'\x00\x00\x00\x01' + socket.inet_aton(SERVER[0]) + struct.pack('!H', SERVER[1])
        self.t.sendto(hdr + data, self.relay)
    def datagram_received(self, d, addr):
        if d[0:3] != b'\x00\x00\x00' or d[3] != 1:
            return
        self.proto.datagram_received(d[10:], SERVER)   # strip the 10 byte header
The lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.
The lab client sent one request:
POST /login   (body: user=alice&pw=hunter2)
user-agent: h3-lab-client/1.0
accept: application/json
authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.demo.token
cookie: session=abc123def456; theme=dark
x-demo: first
What the proxy sees: ten rows for one request
Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.
The host column shows h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column says QUIC.
The thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:
The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.
Filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.
The SETTINGS frame
With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:
Read it against the bytes:
00            stream type: control
04 09         frame type SETTINGS, length 9
01 50 00      setting 0x01 (QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY) = 4096
07 10         setting 0x07 (QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS)    = 16
08 01         setting 0x08 (ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL)  = 1
21 01         a reserved ("GREASE") setting
The 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.
Reading the request
Now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:
You can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:
- A static table. 99 predefined header fields, for example :method GET or content-type application/json. A whole header becomes one small number.
- Huffman coding for strings that are not in the table. QPACK uses the Huffman table from HPACK without changes.
- A dynamic table. A table that grows during the connection. Both ends fill it in using the two QPACK streams (02 and 03). We will come back to this.
The HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:
The core of InterceptSuite shows HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.
Editing the request in flight
Turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.
When the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue says 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.
Then press Forward. The server printed this:
SERVER got POST /login x-demo= tampered body= b'user=admin&pw=letmein'
So the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.
In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:
Two practical points from doing this:
- Every chunk is held, not only the request. The small stream packets (02, 03, the control stream) are held too, one by one. After you forward the request, the queue still has items. Press Forward until it is empty.
- Your client has its own timeouts. If you take too long to edit, the client may give up and close the connection. Edit fast, or raise the timeout in the client you test.
What happens to the bytes when you edit
The extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a new HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:
- The headers are written again with the static table only and plain (not Huffman) strings. Required Insert Count is set to zero. This means the new header block does not depend on the dynamic table.
- If the body changes, it builds a new DATA frame. If the request has a content-length header, it updates that number too. If there is a content-encoding, it compresses the new body again.
- The frame lengths are calculated again, so the HTTP/3 framing stays valid.
- If it cannot do this safely (for example the body is binary, or it is cut off, or it continues in a later entry), it changes nothing. It never sends half-built bytes.
The hard part: the QPACK dynamic table
This is the part that needs care. So far everything decoded nicely. Now send more requests on the same connection (same headers, different path) and look again.
The sizes tell the story. Requests 1 and 2 were 122 bytes each. Request 3 was 13 bytes. And at some point, a 114-byte entry showed up on the client's QPACK encoder stream.
Here are the 13 bytes of request 3, the way they were on the wire:
01 0B 08 86 D1 D7 10 11 12 13 14 15 16
- 01 0B is a HEADERS frame, 11 bytes long.
- 08 86 is the QPACK block prefix: the Required Insert Count and the Delta Base. A Required Insert Count that is not zero means this header block needs entries from the dynamic table.
- D1 and D7 are two entries from the static table (:method GET and :scheme https).
- 10 11 12 13 14 15 16 are seven "indexed field line with post-base index" instructions. Each one points to an entry in the dynamic table. The request says "use entries 0 to 6" and nothing else.
Where are the entries? In the 114-byte entry on the encoder stream. Its first bytes are C0 88 9D 95 E8 1C 6B A4 A8 4F, which is "insert :authority, with a Huffman-coded value" (the value decodes to h3.lab.test). The client sent the long header values once, and every later request only sends numbers. This is a good design. It is also what makes interception harder.
Look at what the HTTP/3 tab shows for request 3:
GET https:// HTTP/3
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 0]:
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 1]:
...
[dynamic table entry (post-base) 6]:
The path, the host, the cookie and the token are gone. That is not a bug in the display, it is the nature of QPACK. The values for these entries were sent earlier, on a different stream. A single history row does not contain them. The extension decodes one entry at a time and does not keep the QPACK table of the connection, so it can only show placeholders.
The server's response did the same thing. After a few responses, its header block started using the dynamic table, and the HTTP/3 tab shows the body but only placeholders for two of the headers:
There is one more thing to see here. In the capture, the 13-byte request (row 30) arrived before the 114-byte encoder stream entry (row 31). That is allowed by design. QPACK lets a request stream wait ("block") until the inserts it needs have arrived. The server announced it could keep up to 16 blocked streams (the QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting we saw above). Later a single byte 88 comes back from the server on its decoder stream. That is a Section Acknowledgment for stream 8, which was the third request: the decoder tells the encoder it processed a header block that needed the table (RFC 9204, section 4.4.1).
So two things follow for a tester:
- You cannot edit these requests with the extension. From the source: if a header block uses the dynamic table, the extension does not rebuild it, and your edit is not applied.
- The data is not lost. The values are in the encoder stream entry in Hex view, and in the raw bytes. You can still forward, drop, and replay them. You just cannot read them as text.
How do you work around it?
- Use the start of a connection. In the lab, the first two requests did not use the table at all, because the client had not inserted anything yet. Whether that holds for your client depends on its QPACK encoder, so check it.
- Replay on a fresh connection, with an edit. A new QUIC connection starts with an empty table. When you edit a request in the HTTP/3 tab, the extension writes it with the static table only, so it does not depend on any earlier state. The next section does exactly this, and the server answers.
- Do not replay a dynamic-table request unchanged. If you send the 13-byte request from Replay on a new connection, the server never answers and never logs the request. That fits how QPACK works. The request points to table entries that this new connection never received, so it cannot be read.
- Look at the encoder stream. It has the real values, in Huffman form. If you must read them, decode the Huffman strings by hand or write a small extension that tracks the table.

The session opens with the details filled in: host, port, protocol QUIC, ALPN h3, New bidirectional stream, and End stream (FIN) ticked. Apple adds ‘face unlock’ to the iPhone Duo, but it’s not Face ID
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
19:26:55 UTC
04:26:55 KST

One of the top complaints from tech reviewers about Apple’s new foldable, the iPhone Duo, has been its reliance on Touch ID, a technology that’s been largely replaced by Face ID across the company’s iPhone lineup.
With Monday’s release of iOS 27.3 beta for developers, Apple is addressing that complaint with a new “face unlock” feature that lets iPhone Duo users unlock their phones using the front camera, rather than waiting for a future hardware upgrade.
To be clear, this feature is not Face ID.
Due to hardware constraints, the iPhone Duo shipped without support for Face ID technology primarily because its thin, foldable design doesn’t offer enough space for the TrueDepth sensor array that Face ID requires. A recent report from Bloomberg suggests that the company is working to change that in a future version of the iPhone Duo. In the meantime, the Duo uses Touch ID for unlocking, authentication, and Apple Pay.
The new face unlock feature, however, will allow users to quickly unlock the device using the front camera when the phone is closed. It only works if users have recently authenticated with Touch ID or a passcode. Apple notes that Apple Pay and passwords will still require Touch ID, and users will have to authenticate with Touch ID again after 45 minutes of inactivity.
The move is meant to make it easier for people to use the Duo in the way they’re accustomed to, after years of unlocking an iPhone just by looking at it.
Apple isn’t going so far as to allow face unlock to work across the entire device, though, because the technology isn’t as secure as Face ID. The latter uses Apple’s TrueDepth 3D sensing hardware, which includes a flood illuminator and a dot projector that casts over 30,000 invisible infrared dots onto the user’s face to build a unique 3D map of the face. The system combines this map with attention-awareness checks, making it resistant to attempts to fool it with photos or other 2D images.
The software update addresses another complaint by incorporating one of the “hacks” iPhone Duo early adopters were using to force their phone to lock when they shut it. That involved creating a shortcut that would automatically run when the phone was closed. Now, Apple says users can enable this feature directly in Settings, under Display and Brightness.
Alongside the software update, Apple announced that more than 200,000 apps are now optimized for the iPhone Duo, up from over 100,000 earlier this month.
Other new features in this latest software release include an option to ask Siri questions about the content of a web page, even portions that aren’t visible without scrolling. Apple is also introducing video podcasts in Apple Podcasts in the Apple TV app, catching up with rivals like YouTube and Spotify.
Apple is also expanding access to Apple News puzzles for News+ subscribers in Australia, the U.K., and for French-Canadian users. Australian News+ subscribers will get access to a daily quick crossword, crossword mini, and Sudoku, as well as Apple’s original puzzles, Quartiles and Emoji Game. U.K. users will get the quick crossword, the crossword mini, and Sudoku, while French-Canadian subscribers will get access to Apple’s original puzzles.
The iOS 27.3 software update is currently available to developers and will soon arrive for public beta testers. It will roll out more broadly to all users after further testing is complete.

OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
19:23:45 UTC
04:23:45 KST

OpenAI is announcing a tool that it says will help child sexual abuse investigators cut through the noise to find harmful material they can act on quickly.
OpenAI wants to stop deepfakes from overwhelming child abuse tiplines
The classifier flagged fewer false positives for humans to review, while getting better at identifying abusive content.
At a Monday press briefing in Washington, DC, OpenAI announced a classifier it says can better detect abusive imagery of kids, including whether it’s AI-generated. It’s also offering free access to vetted organizations, giving developers more guidance on how to detect this type of content, and helping to train law enforcement on how AI can aid their investigations. The news comes as policymakers and others are pushing for more safety restrictions on AI tools, accusing OpenAI and other companies of facilitating harm to children.
In recent years, AI-generated sexual images of children have threatened to overwhelm systems like the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) CyberTipline, which collects and triages reports of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The CyberTipline received 400,000 generative AI-related reports in 2025, an exponential increase from the 67,000 it received in 2024, and researchers have warned that the influx could make NCMEC’s workload “unmanageable.” The US government has stated that both AI-generated and non-AI-generated CSAM is illegal, and 48 states have laws to address sexually explicit AI deepfakes. But the tools to make them are widely available, and researchers say that a flood of fake images can make it harder to tell when a child is actively experiencing harm.
The influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive”
North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who cochairs the AG Alliance’s AI Task Force, said at OpenAI’s event that the influx of AI-generated CSAM reports to NCMEC is “explosive” — and if they keep going that way, “it is going to mean that we fail in our mission.” Tech companies are facing a range of policy proposals that could require them to take more action against CSAM and other potentially harmful content for kids. The Take It Down Act now requires social media platforms to remove real or AI-generated nonconsensual intimate images within 48 hours, and the newly elected Congress could seek to take stronger action against AI companies like SpaceXSI, whose Grok chatbot went on an undressing spree earlier this year. Last month eight states sued OpenAI for a separate set of alleged harms to children, citing lawsuits alleging ChatGPT encouraged illegal substance use and suicide.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images, while the images it did identify were twice as likely to contain abusive material. It’s designed to catch abusive AI-generated images produced by a variety of tools, including open-source models and nudifying apps. It’s also the first broadly available CSAM classifier with a specific flag for AI-generated material, said OpenAI’s head of child safety public policy, John Buckley, at the briefing. “It’s important for industry to be able to understand what images may contain a fictional child versus a real child,” Buckley added. “That triage is critical in law enforcement reporting flows.” He also emphasized, however, that laws should recognize the harm of AI-generated CSAM: “It potentially erodes social norms in offending against children, and it’s often found colocated with child sexual abuse imagery of real children,” Buckley said.
OpenAI says its classifier dramatically cuts down on false positives, flagging 48 percent fewer images
OpenAI’s own ChatGPT image generator is designed to deny user requests for CSAM. Now, users who attempt to produce it will be shown a new warning developed with expert guidance to try to encourage them to seek help. A first offense will trigger a 24-hour pause in accessing ChatGPT and warn the user their account could be permanently closed, while offering support resources to combat the behavior. OpenAI says it reports “all instances of CSAM” to NCMEC. In a statement, Buckley explained that the 24-hour pause is based on expert advice for best practices “and international evidence on what works to prevent and respond to CSAM seeking vs CSAM generation.” The point is “to interrupt harmful behavior and direct people toward specialist help to stop it.”
Jackson said that North Carolina and many other states now have laws that cover synthetic CSAM, but that partnering with a tech company like OpenAI to help deter its creation is a fairly novel approach to an emerging issue. “Most of what AGs do is accountability work,” he told reporters at the briefing. “Most of our jurisdiction kicks in after the fact to hold people accountable for harm. But with this, we wanted to see if it was possible to develop a model of working together to prevent that harm. And I would say it’s still basically an experiment.”

Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing (propublica.org) 80
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."

Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:54:18 UTC
03:54:18 KST

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.
This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel, Databricks, and Microsoft.
Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.
“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.
“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”
With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.
“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.
What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.
Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.
The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.
Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.
Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.
The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.
The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

The Poignant Animation ‘Paper Trail’ Chronicles a Life in Handwriting
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by Don Hertzfeldt, the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.
Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The company announced Monday that it will spend €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its Berlin gigafactory, with plans to begin building Cybercabs there in 2029. The new building in Grünheide, just east of Berlin, will be capable of producing up to 1 million vehicles per year, André Thierig, Tesla’s senior director of manufacturing for the site, wrote on LinkedIn.
Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027. The expansion will make the facility the most technologically advanced of all Tesla factories, Thierig added.
Tesla has been directing more resources toward the Cybercab project, a reflection of its mission to become an AI and robotics company, rather than just an automaker.
The company has already announced plans to cease production of the Cybertruck next year, in part to make room for Cybercab manufacturing at its factory in Austin, Texas.
Musk doesn’t see much of a future for drive-it-yourself EVs even though demand for the Model 3 and Model Y has remained strong despite flagging U.S. sales. The company delivered more than 486,000 vehicles in the third quarter, about 6,000 more than the second quarter. Sales in Europe have been rising as EV adoption continues apace.
Musk has been far more interested in pushing the company toward fully automated driving systems that don’t require a human driver to pay attention — unlike the company’s current advanced driver assistance system, known as Full Self-Driving (Supervised).
The steering wheel-free Cybercab, which was first revealed in 2024 and launched publicly in September, is the current centerpiece of that plan. It’s notable for its lack of a steering wheel, pedals, and other traditional motor vehicle equipment, some of which is required under federal safety standards. (Federal regulators are currently investigating Tesla’s self-certification of the vehicle.)
Tesla’s approach to self-driving systems differs from that of competitors such as Waymo. Tesla relies solely on cameras, rather than additional other sensors such as lidar, to help provide its self-driving system the means to understand its environment. Camera data mimics human vision, but without sufficient training, AI models can struggle to interpret situations that additional sensor data might help clarify.
Tesla has so far taken a slow approach to its Cybercab rollout. The vehicles have been restricted from driving late at night, though Tesla has been working to extend their operating hours. In the more than two months that Cybercabs have been operating, they haven’t had any major incidents.
That track record appears to have given Tesla enough confidence to commit significant resources to expanding Cybercab production and availability. Tesla has about 1,307 robotaxis registered in Texas. Most are modified Model Y vehicles that are used in robotaxi services in several Texas cities. But the Cybercab numbers are growing with about 573 on roads in Austin and soon Dallas.
Now, Europe is firmly on its roadmap, too.

Software is breaking down at a systemic level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:17:17 UTC
03:17:17 KST

Software is breaking down at a systemic level
Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?
This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.
Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.
And then there was the eMudhra fiasco, where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.
It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?
You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.
I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.
But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.
What does it mean for a failure to be systemic?
Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.
Microsoft
The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.
Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.
Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism:
Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.
Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.
His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.
The PHP event
On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website. Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.
It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.
The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.
Shai Hulud attack, May 2026
Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).
These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.
When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens.
The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies.
Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code.
In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.
How we lost control
It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry.
Building software was hard. Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different.
It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand.
But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money.
Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much.
About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries.
Cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic.
Companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops.
And then, we had the Open Source boom.
It was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json, hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet.
Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever.
This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it.
Open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t)
But the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble.
The cultural change
Because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists.
This changed the balance of power between workers and management.
Imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage.
Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong.
By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points.
The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects.
But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor, technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe.
And then AI came in
…And, yes, then AI.
A lot has been written about how AI systems are inherently non-deterministic, a kind of slot machine that only creates simulacra of work. Acting like a stochastic parrot, this argument goes, AI generated code will always be prone to hallucinations and bugs.
And there’s truth to that. But I think the danger in the present moment is the opposite. It’s not so much that the model outputs are crap and unreliable. They’re actually pretty good at doing what you ask them to do (though I suspect that mostly works because Anthropic and co heavily subsidise compute).
I think the real AI threat is decoherence.
Kristen Maevyn wrote an essay named The Decoherence Trap which talks about a problem where the individual parts of a system may look fine in isolation, but don’t make sense as part of a larger system.
Decoherence: the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects.
Software engineers, as I’ve seen them working over the last year, have all but turned over all their work to AI agents. It started with small tasks like writing tests, functions, and individual components. But now it’s everything - not only the components, but the design, the orchestration, the whole concept.
Programming was the activity of translating ideas and intents from the messy human world into code so crystalline, so precise and pedantic, that even a computer could execute it. It was fundamentally the act of distilling complexity into order, making something real out of nothing.
This activity is rapidly dying. It no longer happens in most tech companies.
Most SWEs now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent - they just can’t keep on top of the complexity. Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels - we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.
Kristen writes:
Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable.
A form of learned helplessness has emerged, along with a paradoxical false confidence, caused by the ways LLMs provide the illusion of work without actually forcing us to think through the details.
This de-skilling of software engineers only shifts the balance of power even further away from developers - who can no longer raise the alarm. At its worst, AI turns tech workers into “meat proxies” who spend their days massaging prompts and letting Claude figure out if the work is actually complete.
Systemic decay
It’s not just programmers. It’s the whole chain, top to bottom. Everyone is using AI, especially in big tech.
Claude generates code because the engineer wrote a prompt. The prompt comes from a ticket that was written with Claude. The project manager wrote the ticket based on a summary of a document, that was written by, and then summarised back, by Claude. The document uses statistics from a calculation, by Claude. The business is panicking about the stock market, and the stock market prioritises short term trends over long term engineering.
Does this sound accurate? It’s a caricature, but not by a lot.
I believe that tech companies risk losing their “organisational cognition” - their ability to think and respond as a coherent unit.
This is the real threat: a scenario where nothing in the system is done with intent, and nobody in the system has control. We generate complexity faster than we can tame it.
Look at the problems I’ve outlined. They are about systems of excessive complexity, made of parts that need to work perfectly or else everything falls apart. These parts are being individually corroded by corner-cutting, cost-cutting, overcomplication, over-reliance on uncompensated work and - I fear - helplessness amongst the people who build digital infrastructure.
What is at stake?
This is a threat to all of us. The tech industry is now critical to everyday life. It’s the software that controls your flights, your banking, your petrol pumps, your TV, your payroll. It’s what allows you to navigate roads and find your friends. It’s how you date and how you eat. It’s how you’re reading this.
Society has extended trust, too much trust, into technical systems that are now demonstrating systemic deterioration. I do not think society, government, or institutions are prepared for a world where the incidents and outages of 2026 become commonplace. They too are extending the chain of dependencies, assumptions, complexity and unwarranted trust. Each layer, each link in the chain is a new point of attack that can subvert everything on top of it.
The internet is at a breaking point. The software we build is not legible enough to bear the responsibility the world is giving it. We are telling ourselves the AI revolution is succeeding, precisely because of the rate at which we are generating complexity. The actual load-bearing parts of the ecosystem - open source, engineering-led judgement - are crumbling away.
I think we are only at the beginning of a very painful phase. This is not a blip, and it’s not an aberration - it’s the new normal.

Some OLED MacBook Pro Owners Report Eye Strain and Dizziness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:16:18 UTC
03:16:18 KST

Some owners of Apple's new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display say they experience eye strain, headaches, and dizziness when using the laptop, with affected users pointing to the screen's brightness-control system as a possible explanation.
A significant number of complaints have appeared on Reddit, X, and the MacRumors forums since the new models launched earlier this month. The discussions on MacRumors include a dedicated PWM thread, a separate owner poll, and comments in the reviews and display-details threads.
On X, one user said trying the PROLED MacBook Pro in an Apple Store for around 30 minutes left them with a severe headache. The user said they had previously struggled with OLED screens before finding newer implementations tolerable, and called for an option to change the Mac's dimming behavior.
A Reddit user described how reading text, especially against a black background, brought on dizziness and nausea. They said their OLED iPad Pro did not produce the same symptoms. In the main MacRumors forum thread, a 16-inch PROLED owner reported a headache and mild nausea that began to ease after switching back to a mini-LED MacBook Pro. Another member, posting in the separate poll thread, said they were returning their PROLED laptop for similar reasons after previously having no difficulty with OLED devices.
The suspected issue is pulse width modulation (PWM). An OLED screen produces light through its individual pixels. With PWM dimming, the display changes the time spent at brighter and darker levels during a rapidly repeating cycle. Spending less time at the brighter level reduces the average amount of light reaching the viewer, making the screen look dimmer.
Those fluctuations can occur too quickly to look like an obvious flashing screen, but some people report discomfort with displays that use them. PWM frequency describes how often the brightness cycle repeats. It is different from refresh rate, which is how often the displayed image updates, so a 120Hz ProMotion specification does not tell you the screen's PWM frequency.
Notebookcheck's testing of the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro recorded 240Hz flickering whenever brightness was set to 99% or lower, with a measured amplitude of 56%. In other words, the light output fluctuated 240 times per second, and the amplitude describes the size of those fluctuations. The publication warned that sensitive users could experience eye strain or headaches due to the specification.
Mini-LED MacBook Pro displays also use brightness modulation, but Notebookcheck measured a much higher frequency of 14,880Hz on the 14-inch M4 Pro model. Such rapid fluctuations are generally less likely to cause discomfort for PWM-sensitive users.
Apple already provides a Display Pulse Smoothing accessibility option on supported iPhones. The setting offers another way to dim the OLED screen at low brightness, although Apple cautions that it can affect display performance under some conditions. macOS does not offer an equivalent control, but Apple could add one in the future.
The OLED MacBook Pro models start at $2,899 for the 14-inch version and $3,399 for the 16-inch version. Apple continues to sell the mini-LED models alongside them.

FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:12:21 UTC
03:12:21 KST

The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry.
In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory, the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks.
Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that make it far more difficult for human defenders to keep up.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise “in under three hours.”
The FBI’s warning comes as AI-powered hacks are escalating, particularly by finding easy-to-find security flaws and breaking into companies with relative ease.
Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim’s network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information.
The FBI’s advisory noted that Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool’s first public debut in July. Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions, blamed in large part on weak cybersecurity defenses and lacking protections, such as multi-factor authentication. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.
The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.
A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to a request for comment about the FBI’s claim.
Cybersecurity company Barracuda also disclosed that it was breached as part of an Artex-linked attack by financially motivated criminals, in which the tool found an exposed credential belonging to a third-party service that Barracuda had not revoked when it ended work with the vendor. That access allowed the hackers to access stores of credentials used by Barracuda to collect data from its customers’ systems. Barracuda said it couldn’t rule out access, as its logs were not detailed enough, and chose to “assume the worst” and changed all of its customer credentials.
“Defenders who rely on spotting malicious activity and then responding to it will often arrive after the attacker has finished,” wrote Barracuda’s chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen.
A spokesperson for Barracuda told TechCrunch that the company “directly notified and advised a minority of XDR customers to revoke and recreate integration credentials,” but did not specify how many customers.
After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool’s developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open source version continues to circulate and remains “widely accessible” for use in cyberattacks.
It’s not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration — including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.
Updated with response from Barracuda.

Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be ‘fine’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:11:10 UTC
03:11:10 KST

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.
Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.
Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.
Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.
When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”
He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.
“It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”
OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.
Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.
“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”
Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.
“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:04:55 UTC
03:04:55 KST

Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found.
The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom.
Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers’ power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public.
The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers—the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI.
“Hyperscalers have been growing fast, even before the AI boom,” says Jon Koomey, an energy researcher who was not a part of the study.
To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities’ energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities’ carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa—the first of which is home to Data Center Alley—were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study.
“Knowing for certain data centers how much they use over a year is a really useful thing,” says Koomey, who notes that a peer-reviewed study is more rigorous than some back-of-the envelope calculations. Koomey has been involved in a regular report from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory since 2007 that approximates the energy and water use of the industry. “Sometimes we know it, but sometimes it’s behind an NDA, and no one ever sees it.”
While based on recent data, the study may already be outdated—a reflection of how fast the data center industry is moving. The average size of a facility in the new study is 40 megawatts, which is relatively small compared to some of the data centers under development today. Developers are building campuses that are hundreds or even thousands of megawatts, and there are proposals for still larger data centers.
“Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset,” says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard’s T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.
The study also does not look at developers who choose to build power plants onsite, known as behind-the-meter power—a factor Koomey calls a “wild card” in accurately assessing total data center power use. Plans for behind-the-meter power generation have skyrocketed at proposed data center sites across the US over the past year, with as many as 189 gigawatts in the pipeline earmarked for data centers alone. Many of these plants rely increasingly on inefficient natural gas turbines. BloombergNEF estimated last week that if all of the behind-the-meter power plants in the development queue in the US get built, it could increase overall US emissions by 10 percent.
While the federal government hasn’t tracked data center energy use to date, that could change soon, and it could be a boon to researchers and the public. The Energy Information Agency, the arm of the federal government that tracks energy use across various sectors, conducted three pilot surveys of data center power use across 10 states this year. Those pilot surveys are now complete, EIA spokesperson Lee Tucker tells WIRED, and the agency is currently using them to design a potential voluntary survey for the sector.

SpaceX Catches Starship On the First Try
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

SpaceX Catches Starship On the First Try (theregister.com) 73
			
		 	
				Over the weekend, SpaceX successfully caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit for the first time, demonstrating a key piece of its plan for a fully and rapidly reusable launch system. The achievement means SpaceX has now demonstrated tower catches of both Starship stages, though not yet on the same flight. "Many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)," noted SpaceX's Elon Musk. The Register reports:  Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said.
The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left.

Salsa Macha Mac and Cheese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Salsa Macha Mac and Cheese
The creamy classic gets a Mexican twist just in time for the holiday.
Serves6 to 8
Prep10 minutes
Cook40 minutes
Why You’ll Love Salsa Macha Mac and Cheese
- A savory, spicy and unique spin on the classic. This twist on baked mac and cheese is made with tomato sauce, evaporated milk, and a touch of salsa macha for a deeper hint of heat.
- It’s easy to make. This recipe doesn’t require any complex techniques in order to come together for the holiday table.
As a young wife and mother, my mom learned a pasta recipe from a neighbor, who called it “pasta rapida,” or “quick pasta.” It blended the pasta sauce together, marrying the creaminess and sweetness of evaporated milk and the earthy umami of tomato sauce, and bound it with fistfuls of creamy melted shredded cheese. Looking back, I’d say that’s our Mexican version of mac and cheese.
To take that even a step further this holiday season, the dish gets color from a spicy touch of salsa macha. I also altered the sauce a bit from the original too, adding a couple of boiled carrots, for a creamier texture and a whisper of sweetness to balance the tomato’s acid. Finish with a crispy layer of golden cheese on top, just like the classic baked mac and cheese.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This mac and cheese is perfect for those who love a classic baked mac and cheese but are looking to shake it up a bit! It’s extremely flavorful, gets a delicious crispy cheese top, and stays gooey and cheesy all at the same time. All my friends loved this one!” —Topher, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
I’m a Mexican American food writer and recipe developer of over 6 years. In May of 2025 my cookbook, Make It Plant-Based! Mexican, featuring over 50 vegan Mexican recipes for the beginner home cook, debuted and was featured in Bon Appétit. I consider myself a proud home cook with vegan roots, a strong regional Mexican foundation, and a whimsical bent in the kitchen, with many years in the restaurant industry.
Key Ingredients in Salsa Macha Mac and Cheese
- Carrots: It might sound strange, but what makes this particular recipe sing is the sweet and earthy addition of boiled orange carrots.
- Salsa macha: Key to the spicy element, this salsa fries every element in hot oil, making it ultra-flavorful, aromatic, and rich. You can use store-bought salsa macha or our homemade version.
- Pasta: Fusilli, medium shells, elbow macaroni, rigatoni, and cavatappi are all great choices for pasta that give the sauce and cheese somewhere to cling!
- Evaporated milk: Full-bodied and creamy, it adds a super-rich element to the sauce.
- Tomato sauce: Uncommon in traditional mac and cheese, but it’s the ingredient that makes this recipe shine. Not only does it add color to the sauce, but it also gives it an earthy base and acidic punch that cuts through all that creaminess.
- Grated cheese: Shredded Mexican blend cheese is the ideal combination here, as it’s most typical. However, to bring even more creaminess to this dish, I’d suggest using freshly grated cheese (try a blend of Monterey Jack and cheddar).
Salsa Macha Mac and Cheese Recipe
The creamy classic gets a Mexican twist just in time for the holiday.
Prep time 10 minutes
Cook time 40 minutes
Serves 6 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- 1 pound dried fusilli, medium shell, or elbow macaroni pasta
- 2 small carrots (10 ounces), peeled and left whole
- 1/4 medium white onion, peeled
- 1 clove garlic, smashed and peeled
- 2 (8-ounce) cans tomato sauce
- 1 (12-ounce) can evaporated milk
- 10 sprigs fresh cilantro, plus more for garnish
- 2 teaspoons kosher salt, plus more for the pasta
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 tablespoon Salsa Macha, plus more for garnish
- 1 pound shredded Mexican blend cheese (4 cups), divided
Instructions
- Heat the oven to 350°F.
- Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add 1 pound dried fusilli pasta and 2 peeled small carrots, and cook according to the package directions until the pasta is al dente.
- Reserve 1 cup of the pasta water. Drain the pasta and carrots; reserve the pot. Transfer the carrots to a blender. Rinse the pasta under cool water until cool.
- Add 1/4 peeled medium white onion, 1 smashed and peeled garlic clove, 2 (8-ounce) cans tomato sauce, 1 (12-ounce) can evaporated milk, 10 fresh cilantro sprigs, and 2 teaspoons kosher salt to the blender, and blend until smooth.
- Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in the reserved pot over medium heat until shimmering. Add 1 tablespoon salsa macha and the blended mixture, and cook, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, heated through, and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, about 3 minutes. Stir in the pasta until evenly coated, adding a splash of the reserved pasta water if the pasta is dry.
- Stir in 8 ounces of the shredded Mexican blend cheese until melted. Transfer to a 9x13-inch baking dish. Sprinkle evenly with the remaining 8 ounces shredded Mexican blend cheese.
- Bake until the top is golden-brown and the edges are bubbling, 20 to 30 minutes. Garnish with more salsa macha and finely chopped fresh cilantro.
Recipe Notes
Storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 4 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. To reheat, drizzle in some milk and heat in a 350°F oven until warmed through, about 20 minutes if refrigerated or 40 minutes if frozen.

The Kottke.org Video Closet
Ok folks, I’m gonna apologize in advance for totally ruining any plans you might have had for the rest of your day. The toughest thing about building the Video Closet was getting repeatedly distracted by videos while I was testing it. Seriously, don’t open this thing if you want to get any work done for the rest of the day!
I also tweaked how video embeds work on the main site: there’s now a play button (plays the video in place), an “open on [service]” button (opens it in a new tab on YT or Vimeo), and, on desktop browsers, a widescreen button that embiggens the video in the current window and plays it (my favorite). I like rolling my own video embeds because the default ones from YT & Vimeo are heavy and include a lot of tracking — and now you can choose three different ways of watching, according to the customs of your people.
