Nvidia was in trouble before the Jensen Huang mess
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:24:09 UTC
00:24:09 KST

Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang. Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes, investing in chips to train AI earlier than most.
But just as he’s leaving, the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia, where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great.
“Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says.
Already, competitors have started to move in.
Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026.
Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia.
Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models.
Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025.
And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes.
Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups.
In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale.
China Challenge
While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms.
Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere.
Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms.
Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says.
Trend Spotting
Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips.
Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch.
Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes.
But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips.
But AI models are now so good at reading and writing code that they can port an AI model over to a competitor's silicon at speed.
Wafer, a startup that uses AI to port models to AMD and then serves them more cheaply, has seen revenue grow spectacularly in recent months, boasts CEO Emilio Andere.
Every time a major new open weight model is released Wafer can have it running on AMD hardware at least 80 percent as efficiently within hours, he says. Andere says AI is getting so capable that his engineers barely have to edit or review the code.
Dan Hutchinson, a veteran chip analyst, says Nvidia may be entering its “Intel swan moment,” referring to the 2019 replacement of engineering-focused CEO Brian Krzanich with its CFO Bob Swan. (Sound familiar? Krzanich also resigned after a relationship with an employee; Huang is alleged to have had multiple.) From there, the company’s focus shifted to sales more than technical progress. Bureaucracy ballooned and revenue tanked.
“Nvidia is now an Intel waiting to happen,” he says.

Robert Pattinson will take on the role of James Bond in Amazon MGM’s first film in the 007 franchise. The next James Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve using a script written by Steven Knight, while Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce.
Robert Pattinson is Amazon’s first James Bond
Bond director Denis Villeneuve and Pattinson already worked together in the upcoming Dune: Part Three.
The upcoming James Bond film will be the first from Amazon, which snapped up the rights to the franchise through its acquisition of MGM Studios in 2021. Amazon later gained creative control over the spy series from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson in 2025 after a years-long stalemate. There hasn’t been a new James Bond film since Daniel Craig’s last installment as the spy in 2021’s No Time to Die.
Pattinson recently starred as To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen in the psychological thriller Primetime, and will appear in Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three later this year. He also played Antinous in The Odyssey. Amazon MGM will now need to find actors to play a new Bond Lady, villain, along with an M and Q, as reported by Deadline.
“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson says in the press release. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

New James Bond Announced and the Name's Pattinson, Robert Pattinson

Robert Pattinson has been announced as the successor to Daniel Craig, becoming the seventh actor to play the role in an official Bond movie.
The news was revealed on the official James Bond social media accounts account on Monday. All earlier content was abruptly wiped from 007 on X and Instagram just before 3pm GMT and a repeating message typed out: “Identity confirmed.”
The film studio then released a first photo of the actor in Bond’s trademark tuxedo with a press release confirming the news and saying Pattinson’s casting will “usher in a new era for one of cinema’s most celebrated characters”.
In a statement Pattinson said: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime … To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”
The announcement came after a drawn-out casting process, in which Pattinson was understood to be on a five-strong shortlist, which included Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner. On Friday suggestions emerged that Pattinson had been offered more favourable contract terms than his rivals, fuelling rumours that he was the strong favourite for the role.
Craig’s final film as Bond was No Time to Die, released in 2021 after being delayed due to the Covid pandemic. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying before a title card promised: “James Bond will return”.
Craig made five Bond films in total, starting with Casino Royale in 2006. During his tenure the franchise became a box-office record-breaker, with 2012’s Skyfall alone taking $1.1bn globally.
Pattinson, 40, is due to appear in the next Bond film, the 26th in the franchise (although two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983, take the total to 28). The as yet untitled project will the first to be shot since Amazon-MGM Studios purchased the rights to the series for more than $1bn in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.
Harry Potter producer David Heyman and Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal will oversee the franchise, while the Dune trilogy’s Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders’ Steven Knight is writing the script.
Pattinson has demonstrated his versatility across a wide variety of roles, earning a reputation as an actor with broad enough appeal to support major blockbuster films while retaining artistic credibility with offbeat and unlikely choices. He first came to notice in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and achieved superstardom opposite Kristen Stewart as vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight film series. He appeared in films directed by David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, Maps to the Stars), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse) and Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and returned to franchise film-making with The Batman in 2022.
The first actor to play Bond on the big screen was Edinburgh-born Sean Connery in 1962’s Dr No. So successful was the film that Connery returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many to be some of the franchise’s finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice. Bond creator Ian Fleming’s preference for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian model George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).
Roger Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, which include The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker and Octopussy. The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a six-year gap preceded Irish actor Pierce Brosnan’s debut in 1995 in GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig’s tenure began.
The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.

US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
15:02:34 UTC
00:02:34 KST

The Trump administration on Monday is preparing to roll out new export controls on AI chips and data centers outside the U.S., seeking to prevent companies, especially those in China, from getting past U.S. export controls by remotely accessing AI infrastructure located in other countries.
Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.
The remote-access rules target companies based in the U.S.’s D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and 18 others.
The U.S. already has rules requiring chip companies to get a license to ship AI chips to companies based in, or owned by any business in, this group of countries.
“This new control is a logical extension of existing controls,” the interim rule reads. “These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models.”
The move comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned amid a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy linked to one of the chipmaker’s customers. The U.S. government has reportedly been wanting to put that customer, Megaspeed, on a special entity list, as it believes the company has been buying thousands of Nvidia chips to provide compute to Chinese businesses to get past existing export-control restrictions.
Reuters reported last week that Chinese AI companies are rushing to secure computing capacity overseas amid fears of tighter restrictions from the U.S.
The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.) The rule also covers indirect access through go-betweens or brokers, and exporters and data center operators are required to keep an eye on their customers’ ownership structures and activities to ensure they aren’t run by anyone from the D:5 group.
The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.” For these countries, however, the license requirements will not apply to chips “destined” for companies based in the U.S.
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Notably, the rule doesn’t apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin’s AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips, and restrict transfers of certain powerful AI models. That May, the Trump administration said it would throw out that framework, arguing that it added unnecessary restrictions on U.S. companies and the country’s allies.
“By making these changes, this IFR prevents the use of certain SI items in data centers and at a computing power level that can be used for training or running of advanced SI models,” the rule reads. “Access to such computing power can be used to train and run advanced SI models capable of supporting military- and intelligence-related activities that could threaten U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.”

Google announced on Monday that it’s rolling out new Maps features that are designed to help people plan trips and everyday tasks using AI. The company is launching the ability for Maps to create trip itineraries and find appointments for users.
The new features reflect a broader shift in how tech companies are positioning AI, which is less as a tool that just answers questions and more as an assistant that can complete tasks on users’ behalf. While many companies have released AI agents to complete these tasks, Google is working to bring that approach into a service that millions of people already use every day.
Google says users can use the navigation platform’s “Ask Maps” tool to build step-by-step trip itineraries and get real-time details about their route right when they pull up directions.
For example, you could use Ask Maps to plan a holiday shopping day trip or something more complex, like a three-day road trip featuring coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Google says. You’ll get a day-by-day itinerary with insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop. Once you’re happy with your itinerary, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.
When you’re ready to head out, you can use Ask Maps to reopen your itinerary or find the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll have access to real-time information, including traffic conditions, business hours, and a look at what the “vibe” is at your next stop, the company says. You could also adjust your schedule by asking Maps to do something like add a scenic viewpoint or lunch stop along your route. You can then tap any destination in your itinerary to get directions and navigate to your next stop.
Additionally, users can use Ask Maps to find beauty, pet care, auto, and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. For example, you could ask: “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will then display open slots across nearby businesses.
The new agentic calling feature arrives as tech companies continue to introduce AI agents designed to handle time-consuming tasks, such as scheduling DMV appointments and making reservations. For example, Meta’s AI agent Muse recently gained the ability to call businesses on users’ behalf.
Google also announced that you can now use Ask Maps to quickly find places on your lists by asking something like: “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?”
The tech giant says the new updates are starting to roll out on Monday on Android and iOS. As part of the news, Google announced that Ask Maps is expanding to 30 countries across Europe, including Spain, Germany, and the U.K.

America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:43:48 UTC
23:43:48 KST

Thirty minutes outside Atlanta, the pilot got on the intercom to announce that something was wrong.
America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.
America’s air traffic control system couldn’t handle a single bad router
Inside the Friday the 13th telecommunications breakdown that stranded 1.5 million flyers, and the chaotic briefings that fueled conspiracy theories instead of public trust.
A communications issue with the Federal Aviation Administration was cascading across the country. The pilot didn’t offer much detail except to say that the issue might affect gate access and connecting flights.
For Amanda Khera, the timing couldn’t be worse. Her family vacation to a small island off the coast of Belize had already turned into a medical scare when her 22-month-old son Rio developed a high fever and had to be rushed to a local clinic. Exhausted, they were trying to get home to Virginia Beach, Virginia, to see his pediatrician and rest in their own bed. First, they had to connect through Atlanta.
“It was honestly pretty scary,” Khera said. “We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”
“We didn’t know if the pilot was flying blind without any access to the control towers, or if planes would run into each other.”
— Amanda Khera
She had every right to be scared. She didn’t know what was going on in the cockpit or on the ground. She had no idea that pilots are trained to follow strict procedures that minimize safety risks during major air traffic control outages. All she knew was that several recent incidents, including a midair collision over Reagan National Airport in 2025 that killed 67 people, have called into question the safety of America’s skies. So she spent the rest of the descent looking out the window for nearby aircraft.
Her flight landed safely. But she deplaned into a terminal frozen in place. More than 600 flights out of Atlanta, including their connection to Norfolk, had been canceled. And no one knew when they would be able to take off because every flight across the United States had been grounded.
On Friday, November 13, the nation’s air traffic control system began to fail. Around 3:15PM ET, pilots and air traffic controllers in the Midwest started reporting difficulty communicating with each other over the radio.
“We’re 11,000 [feet] over Grand Rapids airport, about nine miles to the west,” said the pilot of Allegiant Flight 547, his transmission already becoming garbled. “Unable to get… contact… approach on any [frequency].”
Four minutes later, controllers at Quad Cities Airport in Moline, Illinois, reported similar issues across the region.
“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated,” said one. “It sounds like Chicago Approach is going ATC zero, so it might be worse than we initially thought. We thought it was just here.”
With communication outages spreading around the country, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54PM ET “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” From that moment on, no airplanes were allowed to take off in US airspace.
The sudden halt surprised both pilots and controllers.
“Just a heads up, we went in a national ground stop,” said a controller in Seattle.
“Are you saying national as in Reagan National,” asked one United pilot, “or national in the whole country?”
“Across all en route facilities, they’re having communication issues.”
Like so many of the safety incidents that have plagued the air traffic control system over the last few years, this latest failure began with a fragile and outdated piece of FAA infrastructure. In this case, according to the agency, the faulty system was the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, or FTI.
Built by defense giant L3Harris in the early 2000s, FTI is the data backbone of the entire air traffic control system. It links more than 4,400 aviation facilities and carries the voice and radar data controllers rely on to keep planes separated, bridging the gap between the FAA’s legacy phone-based transmission systems and modern Internet Protocol-based ones.
FTI is scheduled to be replaced in 2028. Until then, L3Harris must make incremental upgrades to keep FTI operational.
“We’re dealing with some communication issues on a larger scale than we initially anticipated.”
— Air traffic controller
One of these upgrades accidentally brought down the entire system, according to The Wall Street Journal. Early in the day, L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. Once activated, however, the router began to flood the network with hundreds of connection attempts every second.
This may have added enough extra load to the system to degrade the whole network’s performance, according to I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University.
Hou explained that telecom networks break pieces of information — radio transmissions or radar coordinates, for example — into data packets small enough to be transmitted over the network and reassembled at the other end.
“When the network is degraded, it may start to lose a small portion of packets,” Hou says. “Since you need all packets to reassemble the data feed, just dropping one out of 10 packets may cause your feed to completely stop.”
Most modern communications apps are built to compensate for packet loss. FaceTime, for example, will blur the video or switch to audio-only to preserve the connection.
Air traffic control doesn’t have that luxury.
“Many NAS [National Air Space] applications … require a highly reliable synchronization source with exceptional stability,” according to FAA technical documentation, which warns that instability may cause widespread failure of critical systems.
FAA technicians believe the El Dorado router’s repeated connection attempts created enough instability within the FTI to cut off radio and radar feeds to 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and several Terminal Radar Approach Controls.
“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on,” Hou says.
“We sometimes call this a cascading failure, meaning that one failed device can cause nearby devices to fail, and so on.”
— I-Hong Hou, professor of electrical and computer engineering at Texas A&M University
L3Harris’s contractors isolated the malfunctioning router and another one at a nearby radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. Once those two routers were taken offline, the network began to stabilize once again.
Four and a half hours later, at 8:15PM ET, the FAA lifted the ground stop. It was the nation’s longest since 9/11, spurring airlines to cancel more than 13,000 flights and delay more than 25,000 more through the weekend, according to FlightAware. And more than 1.5 million passengers were stranded.
Faulty technology created the crisis. The FAA’s hamfisted attempts to reassure the public that everything was okay made the situation worse.
For six hours after the ground stop began, the FAA did not provide any public updates except for a terse, 31-word press release and a single X post. Finally, at 11:30PM ET, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to explain the day’s events.
Instead of providing clarity, however, they issued confusing and sometimes even contradictory statements. Mullin opened the conference with a joke (“Welcome to Friday the 13th, right?”) before confidently declaring that “there is no cyberattack.” Instead, he appeared to blame the outage on the FAA’s modernization project.
“As Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and technology was just overwhelming the older system,” said Mullin.
Mullin’s remark appeared to surprise Duffy, who looked at the ground and shook his head. Mullin later walked the statement back after a reporter’s follow-up question, admitting that “there’s nothing completely certain right now.”
Duffy offered more details but did not exactly give a straight answer. “Our switches and routers actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” he said. “I shouldn’t say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers.”
“I don’t want to rule out nefarious activity,” he later added.
“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin concluded. “We are built to handle crisis like this.”
A follow-up press conference on Saturday afternoon was equally bizarre. It started with piercing audio feedback produced by a faulty microphone, which interrupted Duffy right after he introduced Rebecca Guy, the FAA’s acting chief technology officer.
After a four-minute delay, Duffy continued with the briefing. He floated the potential that contractor “incompetence” had caused the outage. And he demanded that Congress allocate billions more dollars to the FAA so it could complete its modernization efforts — calling its existing $12.5 billion modernization budget a “partial payment.”
The conferences only flamed online rumors that the outage was caused by a cyberattack or a rogue AI tied to the September rollout of the FAA’s new SMART system. (So far, no evidence has emerged for either.)
The problem was compounded by an administration already struggling to command public trust. When cabinet officials offered shifting, improvised explanations from the podium, millions of anxious travelers — and even prominent allies — simply refused to take the government at its word.
“Until proven otherwise, not some presser by our government, I firmly believe this was a DDOS attack,” former National Security Adviser Mike Flynn wrote on X. “This is what was being described by two smart cabinet officials who clearly did not understand the technical nature of what happened.”
Khera and her family didn’t know about the political gamesmanship behind the outage — and frankly, they didn’t care. She just wanted to get out of Atlanta on something other than an airplane.
After a night in one of the last available hotel rooms in Atlanta, she and her family rented a car and drove the nine hours back to Virginia Beach. They made it home late Saturday night.
Because of the FAA’s mishaps, they don’t plan to fly again anytime soon.
“We’ve had enough of planes,” she said. “It will take a couple months and more explanations from the FAA to make sure something like this or worse doesn’t happen again.”
Correction, November 16th: L3Harris contractors replaced an old wired telephone switch with a new fiber data router at the FAA radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, not a wireless one. This story has been updated to reflect that fact.

A 512 KiB binary message teaching chess without a shared language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
14:38:54 UTC
23:38:54 KST

Golden Board
Or Why and How to Teach Chess to Aliens.
Intro
Golden Board is a binary message designed to teach chess to an unknown recipient without a shared language, culture, or prior knowledge of the game. It begins by teaching the format needed to read its own contents.
The full project code and documentation are available on GitHub.
This guide follows that process: recover numbers from the bits, use them to reconstruct pictures and interactions, then learn how those pictures describe chess. One complete game connects the layers, from its physical bits to its final displayed position.
Feedback is always welcome.
Before we dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things about the project.
What does it look like?
              In a nutshell, Golden Board is a sequence of 4,194,304 bits, or 512 KiB of ones and zeros.
              That number suggests arranging them into a 2,048 × 2,048 square.
            
What’s inside?
              The first 64 rows contain 32 drawings, each 64 × 64 cells.
              Together they form the bootstrap: it teaches how to read the rest of
              the message. It's chess-agnostic and can be used to decode other structured messages.
            
The payload below contains visual chess lessons, exercises with feedback, complete games, and the information needed to find, check and display them.
Where did the idea come from?
I took inspiration from messages intended for unknown intelligences, such as the Voyager Golden Record, Lincos, and others.
But instead of sharing scientific knowledge or works of art, Golden Board teaches chess.
Why chess?
Two reasons.
First, a small set of rules opens up an enormous world of possibilities, ideas and beauty.
Second, a game can share more than knowledge: it offers a glimpse of the human mind.
How did I test it?
I ran trials using LLMs as stand-ins for unknown recipients, testing decoding and understanding with raw bits, decoded content, and varying levels of assistance.
Correctly recovering the bytes and understanding the lessons are separate tests. These models already know chess, so correct chess answers alone cannot establish that the message taught them. The trials helped identify ambiguities and improve the design; they do not establish that an unknown intelligence would understand it. Read the trial account.
How did I choose the games?
No set of 64 games is complete.
              I chose games for their chess: brilliant attacks, surprising sacrifices, clever defenses, quiet strategy, and beautiful endings. The PGN anthology contains 64 games, while the binary message omits names, dates, and events.
            
What is it all for?
There is a special joy in sharing something you love.
What could we share with a civilization that knows nothing about us? They might already know our science or lack the context for our art, but chess can be taught from scratch, revealing centuries of human imagination, mistakes, and brilliance.
              Most likely, no one will ever receive this message. But even a small chance that someone might discover a position with a move like
              Bf5 makes the whole thing worth trying.
            
Can you build on it?
Yes. The chess-agnostic bootstrap, binary format and Python tools offer a starting point for teaching other subjects without a shared language or culture. Developers can adapt the system; researchers can use the trials to investigate what works, what fails and why. Source code and documentation.
How to read this guide
            In the source drawings, each cell shows a bit: black represents 1 and white
            represents 0. Decoded pictures are reconstructed from the stored data,
            rather than cropped from the source square.
          
Colors, fine gray guides, and labels are added here to make the pictures easier to read. They are not part of the original message.
The intended recipient can infer these arrangements without visual aids, using bounding boxes, fixed sequence lengths, and other previously learned patterns.
The frame below provides an example; its contents are explained later. The blue area covers a data row and its small marks underneath. The orange area picks out the small number to its left. The green area covers a whole boxed list. The gray guides make individual bit positions easier to count.
Hover over a colored phrase to keep only its matching highlights. Hover over the picture to hide all visual aids.
Reading numbers and pictures
The recipient begins with a clean sequence of bits or a sampled square, and is assumed to be able to count, recognize patterns and write simple programs. Obtaining those cells from a signal or physical object is a separate problem.
The first task is to recover pictures and interactions from the bits. The recipient can then use those displays to learn chess. The bootstrap establishes the reading rules through worked examples; the recipient supplies a program that follows those rules. The message carries data for that program to interpret, not executable code.
The bootstrap is the narrow strip at the top of the view below. The payload area beneath it includes the unused space at the end.
Headers show order and related groups
              Before looking inside each drawing, use its header to locate it in the strip. Each frame repeats
              the same corner mark. Its top row pairs a count of filled cells with a binary numeral to give its global number,
              1–32. A second pair two rows below counts steps within a
              related group. That local count restarts for each group; standalone frames leave its row empty.
            
              Compare these four headers. Frame 6 is sixth overall and second in its related group. Frame 3 stands alone:
            
                Frame 1: global 1 (00000001), group step
                1 (00000001).
              
                Frame 2: global 2 (00000010), group step
                2 (00000010).
              
Frame 3: global 3 (00000011), no local counter.
                Frame 6: global 6 (00000110), group step
                2 (00000010).
              
The corner crop below shows the same received pattern at four rotations:
As drawn
Quarter turn
Half turn
Three-quarter turn
              The repeated corner suggests an orientation to try. Ascending counts, dimensions and checksums test
              whether it remains consistent. The corner alone does not prove orientation or which received state should
              represent 1.
            
Frame 1 of 32: Read numbers by counting
Binary numerals connect a pattern of bits to a quantity. This first frame makes that connection by pairing numbers with cells that can be counted.
                The left-hand stripes contain 0,
                1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and
                15 filled cells. Opposite each stripe, the
                upper four-bit numerals give the same
                quantity: the empty stripe pairs with 0000, and two filled cells pair with
                0010. The
                lower eight-bit numerals repeat the
                quantities with leading zeros.
              
Frame 2 of 32: Identify each bit position
A filled bit contributes a different amount depending on its position. Moving it one place left doubles that contribution. This frame pairs each single-bit pattern with its position number.
                The left column starts with
                00000001 and moves its single filled position one place left on each row, ending with
                10000000. The
                right column counts those positions from
                1 to 8, starting at the rightmost bit. Each horizontal pair belongs together.
              
Every field has a black border with a white inset around its data row. The border fixes the full width even when most positions are empty. The eight-bit patterns therefore stay in one column, while their four-bit position numbers stay in another.
Frame 3 of 32: Read a picture’s dimensions and complement
A picture includes its empty positions as well as its filled ones. Its dimensions preserve the rectangle when the bits are inverted.
The left picture has three rows and five columns. In its first row, the first position is empty and the second position is filled.
                The right picture keeps those same fifteen
                positions but exchanges filled and empty. The
                two numerals below the left picture are
                3 and 5: row count, then column count. Both numerals end at the picture’s right edge.
                They count picture positions, not the source cells used to draw
                the blocks.
              
Frame 4 of 32: Establish row order
Without a shared reading order, the same sequence of values could produce different pictures. The numbered arrangement makes the order explicit.
                The upper arrangement has
                1, 2, 3 on its first row and 4, 5, 6 on its second. The
                lower sequence repeats
                1 through 6. Finish each row from left to right before continuing on the next: this is
                row-major order.
              
Frame 5 of 32: Group eight bits into a byte
A byte is a group of eight bits in a fixed order. This frame connects one compact group to its eight individual bit positions, establishing the unit used by later lengths and checks.
                The upper compact pattern is
                00110101. The arrow below it
                leads to eight separate boxes
                containing the same bits in the same order. Read the single centre
                cell in each box: the first is empty,
                while the third is filled.
              
                The two numerals beneath that row
                are 00000001 and 00001000: one row, eight bit positions. The compact
                group above is one byte; the expanded row shows its eight bits. Together, they establish
                one byte = eight bits. The lower half repeats this correspondence for
                00001011.
              
Frame 6 of 32: Combine high and low bytes
A number spanning several bytes needs a byte order. Exchanging its high and low bytes can change its value, even though each byte still contains the same bits.
                Each row repeats a
                sixteen-bit number at the left as its
                first eight bits in the middle and
                last eight bits at the right. Each has its own
                boundary, so an entirely zero high or low byte remains visible as a field. On the fifth row,
                0001001000110100 splits into 00010010 and 00110100: decimal
                18 and 52.
              
                The first byte counts groups of 256; the second counts the remaining units. That row means 18×256 + 52 = 4,660.
                The next row reverses the bytes and represents 52×256 + 18 = 13,330. This
                is high-byte-first order. The notation u16 means a two-byte nonnegative integer;
                u32 means a four-byte one.
              
Frame 7 of 32: Read dimensions and used payload length
The recipient needs to locate the payload and know how much of the remaining square to read. These four measurements separate the bootstrap, used data and unused reserve.
                Top to bottom, the fields give the
                square side, 2,048;
                the first payload row, 64,
                counting from 0; the
                byte width, 8 bits; and the
                used payload length, 506,509 bytes.
                The first three fields have sixteen bits each; the last has thirty-two. Their right edges align,
                so the wider last field extends farther left.
              
                Starting at row 64, read left to right across each row, then continue on the next.
                Each group of eight cells gives one byte, with its highest-value bit first. Recover exactly
                the declared number of bytes.
                Frame 32 shows how the used length relates to the remaining capacity.
              
Checking the recovered bytes
The recipient needs more than plausible-looking numbers before trusting the recovered lessons and games. A wrong orientation, bit interpretation or byte grouping can still produce values. Golden Board includes checks that let the recipient reject an inconsistent reading before using its content.
The content is organized into documents: collections of picture definitions, numerical data and display or interaction instructions. Each document’s bytes sit inside a checked block called a section. Its header identifies the document and gives its byte length. That length locates both the check at the end and the beginning of the next section.
A section also stores a checksum, a value calculated from its identifying fields and content. The program creating the message computes this value from the original bytes. The recipient repeats the calculation on the recovered bytes and compares the result with the stored check. A mismatch rejects that reading. A match supports the consistency of those bytes; it does not repair them or establish that their meaning has been understood.
              Take section 2 from the actual payload. Its first six bytes form a header:
              the document’s number, called its ID, and
              the document’s byte length.
              The document itself follows,
              then the stored checksum.
              The calculation covers the header and every document byte, and stops before the stored check.
            
Golden Board uses CRC-32C for this calculation. The next drawings teach it with one input byte before applying the same method to a complete section. The immediate goal is to reproduce the sender’s check from the same bits.
Frame 8 of 32: Define XOR and equality
The checksum needs a way to combine bits and a way to test agreement. This frame defines both operations using every possible pair of inputs.
                The left-hand input columns list
                00, 01, 10 and 11. Their
                results are 0,
                1, 1, 0: XOR produces 1 when the inputs differ. The
                right-hand input columns repeat those
                pairs; their results are
                1, 0, 0, 1: equality produces 1 when
                they agree.
              
Frame 9 of 32: Shift right and keep the outgoing bit
A right shift moves each bit one position to the right. This frame separates the shifted row from the bit that leaves its right edge; the checksum calculation uses both results.
                In the upper example, the input field
                ends in 00110101. The
                shifted field beneath it ends in
                00011010. A zero enters at the far left, and the
                separate outgoing-bit box contains
                the 1 that left the input’s right edge.
              
                The other examples repeat this layout with different input patterns. In the lowest example,
                the input ends in 0, and the
                outgoing-bit box has an empty centre.
                Its border preserves the result’s position even when the result is zero.
              
Frame 10 of 32: Identify the checksum’s fixed patterns
Both sender and recipient need the same constants to obtain the same checksum. The following calculations use the patterns shown here.
                The top field contains thirty-two
                ones. The middle field contains
                another thirty-two-bit pattern. The
                bottom field repeats that entire
                middle pattern and adds one leading 1. The fields line up at their right edges,
                making the added bit visible at the left.
              
                The lower fields are two forms of CRC-32C’s polynomial, the fixed pattern that
                identifies this CRC. The bottom form includes its leading bit. Keep the middle pattern for
                comparison with the changes between the states in Frame 12.
              
Frame 11 of 32: Start the checksum and XOR a byte
                The checksum keeps a changing 32-bit working pattern, called its state.
                Combining an input byte with that pattern lets the byte affect the eventual check.
                This frame shows the starting state, the first byte and the result of combining them.
              
                A shared outer box groups the two inputs:
                the all-ones state above and the
                input byte below. The state has four
                eight-bit bands. The input is 00110101, the pattern expanded in Frame 5, aligned under the
                rightmost band.
              
                Applying Frame 8’s XOR rule to those eight aligned positions gives 11001010. The other
                three state bands have no input bits to change and remain all ones. The
                downward arrow leads from the grouped inputs
                to this four-band result. That result starts
                the eight bit rounds shown next.
              
Frame 12 of 32: Follow all eight bit rounds
The recipient must be able to calculate the next checksum state from the current one. This frame supplies a complete worked sequence, so the rule can be checked against every transition.
                The numbers at the right label
                the working patterns, from state 0 to state 9. The
                first row is the starting pattern;
                the second row is the byte-XOR
                result from Frame 11. Its last bit is 0. Shifting that row right
                gives exactly state 2.
              
                State 2’s
                rightmost bit is 1.
                Shift the entire pattern right. The top teal row in the comparison below is
                that calculated shift result. The bootstrap also supplies the next result,
                state 3, shown in
                the middle rose row. Comparing them reveals the extra change made in this round.
              
                Line up matching positions in those two rows. In the
                cyan columns, the bits differ: the shift result has to be
                flipped to produce the supplied result. Put 1 at each differing position and
                0 at every matching position. This is the XOR comparison learned in
                Frame 8. Its bottom row is the fixed feedback pattern: a map of
                which positions to flip.
              
                We used the frame’s supplied result to identify that pattern. To calculate the round forward,
                shift state 2, then XOR the shift result with the feedback pattern. Those flips
                produce state 3. The outgoing 1 selects this feedback step, so the bit
                continues to affect the checksum after leaving the right edge.
              
                The six remaining rounds use
                the same rule. Inspect the rightmost bit before shifting: an outgoing 0 needs
                only the shift; an outgoing 1 also
                needs the fixed XOR pattern. There are eight rounds after the byte-XOR step, ending at state
                9. The table transcribes every supplied state and names the operation that produces it.
              
              The fixed XOR pattern exposed by Frame 12’s transitions is the middle pattern of Frame 10
              read in reverse bit order. This relates the right-shift calculation to the polynomial shown
              there. It changes the interpretation of that constant; the bytes themselves keep the
              high-byte-first order established by Frame 6.
            
Frame 13 of 32: Finish and store the checksum
The last running state becomes a stored checksum through one final XOR. The recipient must distinguish that final value from the intermediate states used during calculation.
                This repeats Frame 11’s grouped-input layout. XOR the
                state after eight rounds with the
                all-ones state above it. The arrow leads to
                the result, whose four bands read
                87 | 111 | 14 | 252.
              
                A second arrow leads to
                four separately bounded bytes. Each sits
                directly below the corresponding band of the result, with the same eight bits. Reading left to right
                preserves high-byte-first order. This is the check for the single input byte 00110101; the
                next frame compares a computed check with a stored one.
              
Frame 14 of 32: Compare computed and stored checks
A checksum becomes an integrity check by comparing the calculated value with a stored one. These three cases show the same equality test succeeding, failing, then succeeding again.
                In the top case, the input field contains
                00110101, read as 53. The
                computed check on the upper line and the
                stored check below it agree. The
                one-bit equality field at the right
                therefore contains 1, using the same boxed-bit convention as Frame 8.
              
                The middle case changes the input to 00110100 but retains the check for the earlier
                pattern. The checks differ, so the equality field contains 0. The bottom case uses
                00001011 with its own check and returns 1. These are checks of byte patterns,
                not of the characters used to print their decimal readings.
              
Finding sections and documents
The recipient can now read numbers and reproduce a checksum. The next task is to find each section’s boundaries and recover the document inside it. The section is the checked storage wrapper; the document is the collection of things to display and use.
Those things are stored as records. Each record has a kind, a numeric name called an ID, and its own contents. For example, one record can define a small picture and another can refer to that picture by ID. Keeping the definition in one place lets many displays reuse it. IDs are assigned during message creation and stored in the data; the recipient reads them rather than inferring them from a shape. Their scope is one document.
An inventory lists the documents that must be recovered and the records where each may be opened. These starting records are its entries. They lead to a picture sequence or an interaction. An entry is a record’s ID, not its byte address.
              To teach these relationships, the bootstrap contains a complete small worked document of
              326 bytes. Its simple pictures and responses exercise the format before chess appears.
              The next drawings describe that example, which is carried inside the strip. The full five-document
              payload below the strip uses the same rules.
            
Frame 15 of 32: Partition a complete section
This frame divides a section into byte ranges. Its header declares how much body data follows, so the recipient can find the check and the next section.
                Every row has three columns: start address, byte length, and the first address after the range. The
                ID row reads 0, 2, 2; the
                body-length-field row reads
                2, 4, 6. Those two fields form the six-byte header. The
                body row reads 6, 326, 332, followed by the
                check row: 332, 4, 336.
              
                The section is therefore 336 bytes: six header bytes, 326 body bytes and four check bytes. These triples
                describe the layout; they are not extra fields stored in the header. The body-length value counts the
                body alone. The ID names the section; its meaning is established by the inventory example below.
              
Frame 16 of 32: Map payload addresses to square cells
Byte addresses must lead back to positions in the square. This frame connects each address to a physical row and column.
                The top line of each box gives a
                byte offset from the payload’s start and a
                bit index within that byte. Directly beneath
                them are the square row and
                square column. These are addresses for reading stored bits, so they start at zero;
                bit 0 is the first, leftmost bit of a byte. The labels in
                Frame 2 instead count binary places from the right, starting at one.
              
                Each physical row holds 2,048 ÷ 8 = 256 bytes. The first group of 256 bytes therefore fills
                row 64: byte 0 starts at column 0, byte 1 at column
                8, and byte 255 ends at column 2,047. Byte
                256 starts the next row, 65, at column 0. These boundary cases appear in the
                third, fourth and fifth boxes.
              
                To locate another byte, count complete groups of 256 to find how many rows to move down from row 64.
                Within the remaining group, move eight columns for each byte, then add its bit index. This is why
                section boundaries need not coincide with physical row boundaries.
              
Frame 17 of 32: Preserve rectangular and empty rows
Dimensions preserve a picture’s complete rectangle, including white positions and entirely empty rows.
                For the upper-left matrix, the
                first numeral above it is
                00000010: two rows of height. The
                next numeral is 00001000:
                eight columns of width. The other boxes use this same order, giving three rows by five columns, one by
                seven, and two by eight.
              
The second row in the lower-right matrix is completely empty. Its eight positions still belong to the picture. Neither the empty row nor the white columns can be removed by cropping to the visible black shape.
Frame 18 of 32: Name objects and count their references
An object can be given a numeric name, then referred to by repeating that name. This frame separates names, reference counts and reference lists, with every target introduced before its use.
Each row has three parts: an eight-bit name on the left, an eight-bit reference count in the middle, and a boxed list on the right. The name does not specify the object’s size or its physical address.
                The top row begins 00000110,
                read as 6. That pattern names the first object. Its count is 00000000, so the
                reference list is empty. The
                second row gives another name,
                00000111 or 7, also with no references.
              
                The third row begins 00001000,
                read as 8. Its count 00000001 says one reference follows:
                00000110, repeating the first row’s name.
              
                The bottom row begins
                00001001, read as 9. Its count 00000010 says two references
                follow: 00000111 and
                00001000. These reach the second and third objects. Following the third object’s own reference then reaches the
                first. Counts and list lengths progress together: zero, zero, one, two.
              
Frame 19 of 32: Check the miniature’s actual section
This frame gives the miniature section’s actual fields and the exact range covered by its checksum. It places the stored check after that range, outside its own calculation.
                The three four-bit numerals on the left
                give the byte counts of the bands beside them: 0010, 0100, 0100
                mean two, four and four bytes. The small marks under the data identify the start of each byte.
                These black numerals and marks belong to the original drawing. They describe how to read its
                bands; they do not add bytes to the section.
              
                The first two data bands give
                section ID 1 and body length 326. The
                third band contains the four
                stored checksum bytes, 255 64 93 120.
              
                The upper bounded range reads
                0 | 332 | 332: start at byte zero, check 332 bytes, stop before address
                332. The result below the arrow
                repeats the stored check’s bits. The
                lower bounded range is
                332 | 4 | 336, locating those four check bytes after the covered range.
              
Carry the checksum across a sequence of bytes
              The covered range contains six header bytes and 326 body bytes. Start with the all-ones
              state, XOR the first byte into its low eight bits, and perform eight rounds. XOR the next byte
              into the resulting state and perform another eight rounds. Continue through every covered byte,
              then apply the final all-ones XOR once. Restart this process for each section. Calculating a
              separate finished checksum for every byte would lose the running state that joins the sequence.
              Frame 29 supplies all the bytes of this worked section.
            
Frame 20 of 32: Read a complete inventory section
The inventory lists the document sections required for a complete message. Here it contains one document: the worked miniature.
                The six-byte header declares section ID
                0 and body length 18. The
                next eighteen bytes are the inventory body,
                followed by its four checksum bytes,
                113 28 238 100. Together they occupy 28 bytes: three full eight-byte rows and half of a
                fourth, starting at local row 31.
              
                The first row contains the header and the beginning of the body. Row breaks are presentation boundaries,
                not section delimiters. ID 0 identifies the inventory; positive IDs identify documents.
                This small inventory lists only the worked document inside the bootstrap.
              
Frame 21 of 32: Read inventory counts and entry references
                The inventory identifies a document to recover and the records where reading it may begin.
                This frame expands the inventory body from Frame 20 into individual fields.
              
                The four-bit byte counts on the left
                use the convention from Frame 19. For example, 0010 beside the first band says
                that its value occupies two bytes. The value in that band is 1: one document.
              
                The first three data bands give
                document count 1, document section ID 1 and document length 326.
                The next band contains
                255 64 93 120, the expected checksum bytes for that document’s section. They match
                the check in Frame 19.
              
                The entry count is 2.
                It gives the length of the boxed list
                of entry IDs 512 and 257. Each entry ID occupies two bytes,
                as its own left-hand count confirms. These IDs name records, rather than byte addresses;
                the next frames define those records.
              
Reading the five record types
Finding a document’s bytes does not yet tell the recipient how to draw its pictures or conduct its exercises. Its records divide that work into five kinds, all using the same named-record format.
              A glyph stores a small rectangular bitmap. A display frame places glyph IDs in a
              larger grid, so the same bitmap can be reused in many cells. A frame cell selects an entire glyph;
              it is distinct from either a source-message cell or one pixel inside the glyph. “Frame N of 32”
              continues to mean a bootstrap drawing; a numbered display-frame record belongs to a document.
            
A trace starts from a frame and applies stored changes to indexed cells. This lets the message show a changing diagram or replay a game without storing every complete picture separately. A page combines a display with choices, accepted responses, feedback destinations and links. A table stores numbers alongside a trace; the lessons teach what those numbers mean.
              The worked document has 15 records: three glyphs, four display frames, one trace,
              one table and six pages. Its header names page 512 and trace 257 as entries.
              Each record begins with its kind, ID and content length; the record’s own contents are also called
              its payload. That length excludes the record’s seven-byte header. Read all the records
              before resolving their references: a target can occur later in the document.
            
The player is the recipient’s program for interpreting these records and carrying out their display and interaction operations. A frame fixes which bitmap belongs in each cell. This guide displays equally sized tiles with enlarged glyphs inside them; tile size and spacing are presentation choices. The encoded dimensions count frame cells and glyph pixels.
Frame 22 of 32: Read a document header and rectangular glyphs
A document provides starting records and reusable bitmaps. This frame first defines its header, then two glyph records.
                The top five data bands contain marker
                bytes 214, 57, entry count 2, record count 15, and entry IDs
                512 and 257. The
                small rulers down the left count bytes. The
                markers below each band identify byte starts. Both are original black marks that describe the
                bands; neither contributes bytes to the serialized document. The table’s Bytes column transcribes
                the left-hand widths.
              
                The middle group and empty rectangle define
                glyph 0; the
                bottom group and patterned rectangle
                define glyph 1. Each record begins with kind 1, a two-byte ID and a four-byte
                payload length. Its three payload bytes give two rows, three columns and a packed bitmap.
              
                Glyph 0 has bitmap byte 00000000, read as 0. Glyph
                1 has 11010100, read as 212. Its first six bits form
                110 / 101; two zero padding bits complete the byte. Both rectangles retain all three
                columns, including white pixels.
              
The document header as bytes
The document begins with these ten bytes, shown in decimal and grouped by field. Two-byte integers are stored high byte first.
214 57 0 2 0 15 2 0 1 1
              The band map identifies the fields in this sequence. Each entry ID takes two bytes: 2 0 is
              512, and 1 1 is 257.
            
Kind 1: a reusable bitmap
              Glyph record 1 occupies miniature bytes 20–29:
              1 0 1 0 0 0 3 2 3 212. Its seven-byte header gives kind, ID and
              payload length. Its three payload bytes give two rows, three columns and mask 212, or
              11010100. The first six bits form 110 / 101; two zero padding bits complete the
              byte.
            
              Glyph 0 is a separate record with an all-zero mask. Both glyphs retain their full two-row,
              three-column dimensions. Their IDs are names that display frames use to select these shapes. A frame cell
              containing 1 therefore selects glyph 1; it does not turn the whole cell into a
              single filled block.
            
Frame 23 of 32: Build a frame from glyph IDs
A display frame builds a larger picture by placing reusable glyphs at indexed positions. It can also assign names to positions that a later exercise lets the recipient select.
                The record header identifies kind
                2, ID 256 and payload length 18. The
                two dimension fields specify two rows and
                three columns. The six glyph IDs are
                0,1,1 / 1,0,1, read across each row. Looking up those IDs produces the
                picture at the lower left. The
                left-hand rulers give each band’s byte
                width.
              
Glyph IDs fit in one byte, so these six frame cells occupy six bytes. Record headers still use two-byte IDs. The width of a reference depends on the field that carries it.
                After those cells, a count of 2 introduces two selection definitions. Each definition
                contains a region ID followed by a cell index. The
                first definition is
                10 | 0: region 10 selects cell 0, the upper-left position. The
                second definition is
                20 | 5: region 20 selects cell 5, the lower-right position. The
                matching highlights connect each pair to its picture position and its index box.
